So also when the Lord Jesus was hung on the Cross He did not fail when He was crushed, nor weaken when He was torn, and when He was pierced by the spear He became more beautiful by the blood poured out of Him, as though He had carried a new beauty that cannot die in itself (a spiritual death) but gives the dead the gift of eternal life. And the Holy Spirit rested upon this flower that budded in the royal rod].

This is our Beloved to us, His bride; He has carried by His sufferings the sweet fragrance, smelled by those in the plain, that is the Jews, and those in the valley, that is the community of the Gentiles... But what are we to Him?
“As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters” [2].

Origen says: [Since He became the lily of the valleys, it was that His beloved also might become a lily imitating Him... that is, every soul that draws near to Him and follows His steps and imitates Him becomes a lily].

St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that the soul like the lily rises straight upward toward the Messiah her true Vinedresser. He lifts her above the cares of this life and the thorns of sin that choke the soul (Mk 4:18), and rises above the dust of this life that she may not be defiled...

The believer in the eyes of the Lord is like the lily, “the lily-flower,” exceedingly splendid, and not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed like it, beautiful not by her own righteousness but by the grace of the blood that runs in her...

Though man has accepted the thorns of sin, so that they surround him on every side, yet the Lord sees him as the lily, comes down to him and passes through the midst of the thorns, and bears the curse for him!

In the Beloved’s address, “As the lily among thorns,” there is also guidance to her that if she wants to be adorned with virtues she must bear the pains of the thorns with care, and as St. Ambrose says: [The virtues are surrounded by thorns of spiritual evil, so that no one can gather the fruit unless he draws near with care].
Origen sees in this saying a true picture of the beautiful Church surrounded by heresies and heretics who want to destroy her...

St. Augustine sees in this expression and its like a declaration of the fewness of the righteous who live in the midst of the world “like a lily among many thorns” until the day of harvest comes and separates the lilies from the thorns.

entries.section: The need for the Beloved:

paragraphs.text: Though the human soul has become like a lily among thorns, she is not occupied with the thorns around her, but with the Bridegroom who satisfies her and waters her and gives her fragrance... She sees Him coming to her, drawing near to her that she may draw near to Him, lifted up on the Cross that she may rest in the shade of His eternal love, and He presents to her the fruit of the Cross, sweetness in her throat; therefore she addresses Him, saying:
“As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. I desired to sit under his shadow, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” [3].

Though she lives among the thorns and cannot rise to Him, He comes down to her, and becomes like the apple tree (a symbol of the divine Incarnation) within her reach. He has dwelt among us, the fruitless thicket, and became one of us, but not fruitless like us, but like the apple tree: beautiful to see, its fragrance refreshing, its fruit eaten, and its juice drunk... He is the tree of life that we pluck instead of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

Truly, the earth has been dry for such a length of time, because we ate from the tree of disobedience, and the Beloved came, “the obedient Son”... He came to us in the midst of our thorns, and entered into our sufferings, and bore the curse of the thorns for us, that we may sit at His feet and take shelter under the Cross of His love in the midst of the severity of the distress of this world.
In the world there are many trees of the thicket that we imagine to be restful for us, but one tree—the spiritual apple tree—has in it all satisfaction.

If “the apple tree” refers to the divine Incarnation, then the trees of the thicket refer to heresies and strange teachings, for there is no rest for us except in the incarnate Word alone, far from every heresy. In this Origen says: [The bride desires to sit under the shade of this apple tree, meaning that the Church, as we said, is under the protection of the Son of God, or that the soul flees from all strange teachings to cleave to the Word of God alone and finds His fruit sweet in her throat, through continual meditation on the law of God, chewing it as though she ruminates it as the clean animal does].

In ancient times the Gentiles sat in the shadow of death (Isa 9:2; Mt 4:16) as they sat under the shadow of the tree of disobedience, but now they enjoy the shadow of the Giver of life by sitting under the shadow of the Cross of obedience.

In ancient times the Jews sat under the shadow of the Law, through the literal, killing understanding. But now it has been given to us to enter under the shadow of Christ by tasting the spiritual understanding of the Law which edifies. And the following is a comparison by Origen between the shadow of the Law and the shadow of Christ:

[It seems that every soul as long as it is in this present life needs a shade, as I think because of the heat of the sun which makes the seed without deep roots wither and die. The shadow of the Law gave a little protection against this heat, but the shadow of Christ under which the Gentiles now live—that is, faith in the Incarnation—gives complete protection from the heat and even extinguishes it. For (Satan), who used to burn the poor who were under the shadow of the Law, was seen falling from heaven like lightning at the time of the passion of Christ. But the time of this shadow is completed at the end of the ages, for as we said, at the end of time we no longer see (Christ) in a mirror nor in a riddle, but face to face].

St. Mary, who represents the Church, as an ideal member in her, sat under the shadow of the Most High through the divine Incarnation, as the angel said to her: “the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God...” By this it has become possible for the believer to sit under the shadow of the Lord and eat His sweet fruit after his mouth had been embittered for a time of such length because of sin. After it was said of himself, “their throat is an open sepulchre” (Ps 5:11), she has come to open her mouth not as a sepulchre bearing the death of sin but rather to eat the Body of the Son of God the Giver of life, and to taste the sweetness of His fruit... She says also: [I opened my mouth, and drew to myself a spirit] (Ps 119:131).

Origen says: [Her saying “and his fruit was sweet to my throat” applies to the soul in whose mouth there is nothing dead or base, and who does not at all resemble those of whom it was said (their throat is an open sepulchre); for such mouths that bring out words of death and perdition are called sepulchres, those that utter words contrary to the true faith, and oppose the order of purity and justice and dignity].

entries.section: In the house of perfect love:

paragraphs.text: When the soul sits with her Beloved at the Cross, and tastes His infinite love, she asks Him to enter into His bowels to be watered from the deep springs of His love, saying:
“He brought me to the house of wine, and his banner over me was love. Stay me with cakes of raisins, comfort me with apples: for I am wounded with love” [4-5].

We have already seen that “the house of wine” is the house of “the new life” that became ours through the saving sufferings of the Lord Christ. The house of wine symbolizes “the house of the feast and of wisdom,” where the soul enters to the Lord Christ and receives the juice of the teachings of truth and its mixture in the vessel of divine wisdom, by which the soul is refreshed anew every day... as she comes to know the mysteries of God as though they were new every day.

In this Origen says: [As for the wine that is extracted from the true Vine, “the Lord Christ,” it is always new, by which the understanding of the learners of spiritual knowledge and wisdom is renewed continually; for this reason Jesus said to His disciples: I will drink this wine with you new in my Father’s kingdom (Mt 26:29), because the understanding of hidden things and the declaration of mysteries is continually renewed through the wisdom of God, and that not only for men, but also for the angels and heavenly powers].

When the loving Lord brings the believing soul into the house of His love and reveals to her the mysteries of His wisdom that are new every day, she understands “love” as a sign of the victory of her Beloved and King, so she sets up “the banner of victory” over her, saying: “his banner over me was love.” He has reigned over her completely by love. But the Septuagint’s rendering of this expression came thus:
“Put in the order of love” [4].

When the soul enters the house of her Beloved she is bound by the law of His house, namely “love,” but since she cannot apply it by herself she asks Him to Himself arrange the life of love in her, that is, she receives from God “true love,” the law of His love, so she knows how to love God and parents and brothers... and so on.

Love has its own ordering: man is bound to love God with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might... that is, to love without reckoning and without limits. And man is bound to love his neighbor as himself (for its salvation), and his love for his brother would be a love that has lost its good ordering. Man is bound to love his parents by honoring them practically in the Lord, as a husband is bound to love his wife in a way that differs from the love of children for parents, and different from the love of shepherds for their people. Truly in “the house of love” we receive the one nature of love from its Source, “God Himself,” but we are bound also to come to know the law of practical love.
The soul returns to cry out, declaring her need of “love,” saying:

entries.section: In the house of perfect love:

paragraphs.text: “Stay me with cakes of raisins (spices), comfort me with apples: for I am wounded with love” [5].

Since the soul has entered “the house of divine love” and received from God the ordering of love, she declares that she has become wounded with love; it is impossible for these wounds to be those of a bodily love, for according to Eastern traditions it is not fitting for the beloved to say that she is wounded with love but for the man alone. And besides, how could the beloved ask others—other than her Beloved—to support her or comfort her?! Can cakes of raisins or spices or apples bind up the wounds of love or heal its sickness?

These are the cries of the soul within the Church, “the house of love,” as she asks the servants of Christ to support her with cakes of raisins or the spices which are the comforting divine teachings that pour the love of Christ within and spread His sweet fragrance. She asks for the apple which is a symbol of the holy Body, for it is the mystery of her spiritual refreshment! For it alone can satisfy the heart with love, and give the soul a good and fitting ordering of love.

As for the secret of the soul’s wounds by love, as Origen says it is Christ Himself, who is the living and effective word of God, sharper than a two-edged sword, who enters into the depths of the soul and wounds her with divine love; and the following are some comments of the Fathers on this expression.
* Would that the unhealthy be wounded, for when they are wounded as is fitting they become healthy!

St. Augustine * Holy Scripture teaches us that God is love (1 Jn 4:8); He aimed His only-begotten Son, “the chosen arrow” (Isa 49:2), at the chosen, planting its threefold point in the spirit of life.

The head of the arrow is faith, which binds the one who shoots the arrow with those struck by it, as though the soul is lifted by divine elevators, so she sees within her the arrow of sweet love wounding her. Adorned with wounds...
It is a good wound and a sweet pain, by which “life” penetrates the soul. For by means of the tears of the “arrow” the soul opens the door that is her entrance...

St. Gregory of Nyssa * If anyone is ever set ablaze with sincere love for the word of God, if he has received one of the sweet wounds of this “chosen arrow” as the prophet calls it, if anyone has been wounded by the spear of His knowledge, worthy of all love, so that he yearns and longs for Him night and day, so that he can speak of no one but Him, nor listen to any but Him, nor think of anything but Him, nor incline to any desire or hope for any other, when it becomes thus the soul says truly: “I am wounded with love.” She receives her wound from the One of whom she says: “He hath made me a chosen arrow, and in his quiver hath he hid me” (Isa 49:2).
It is fitting for God to strike our souls with a wound like this, to wound them with such arrows and spears, to strike them with such healing wounds...
Since God is “love,” they say of themselves: “I am wounded with love.” Truly it is the drama of love when the soul says: I have received the wounds of love!

The soul that is set ablaze with longing for the wisdom of God, that is, that can behold the beauty of His wisdom, says in the same way: “I am wounded with wisdom.” And the soul that contemplates the loftiness of His power and is amazed at the power of His word can say: “I am wounded with power.” I think that such a soul is the very one that said: “The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” (Ps 26). And the soul that is set ablaze with love of the justice of God and contemplates the justice of the ordering of His providence says truly: “I am wounded with justice.” And the soul that looks to the greatness of His goodness and the tenderness of His love speaks likewise. But the wound that includes all these things is the wound of love by which the bride declares: “I am wounded with love.”
Origen

entries.section: In the house of perfect love:

paragraphs.text: These are the wounds of love with which the soul was wounded by “the chosen arrow,” the Lord Christ, who by His love places His left hand under our heads that He may direct them away from temporal things, cutting off in us all love for earthly things, and with His right hand draws us toward heavenly things; therefore the soul addresses Him thus:
“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me” [6].

In other words, with His left hand He disciplines, so that temporal life and all the pleasures of the body and the world become small before us, and with His right hand He shows mercy, as He opens the heart before the heavenly things so that we long for them. In any case, the Lord places His disciplines under our heads, for without them our heads would not be balanced, and surrounds our heads with His right hand so that our hearts are filled with hope in Him! These are the true, healing divine wounds of love.

entries.section: In the house of perfect love:

paragraphs.text: When the soul entered into the house of divine love, and was wounded by the healing arrow, she feels His infinite love whether in His disciplines or His tenderness, and feels through both (discipline and tenderness) as though her head were leaning on His left hand and encircled by His right hand, so her whole being is in His divine embrace while her face is opposite His face, receiving all the kisses of His divine mouth... therefore she is careful that no one cut off these deep fellowships, saying:
“I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and by the hinds (powers) of the fields, that ye stir not up, nor awake the beloved, till he please...” [7].

It is as though she carried the feelings of the Apostle Peter when his depths were wholly drawn toward the Lord Christ transfigured before him, and he said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Mt 17:4).

Certainly, this expression cannot apply to bodily love, for how would the beloved ask her friends not to wake the beloved?! Is this their work? But it is a wonderful picture of the Church the Mother who asks her children, “the daughters of Jerusalem,” to remain in the divine embrace, and not to disturb the Lord who rests in their hearts by committing evil or sin! It is the voice of the Church the Mother toward every believing soul called “a daughter of Jerusalem” who looks to the heavenly Jerusalem as her mother, adjuring her by the powers of her inner field which the Lord blessed! (Gen 27:27), as she is the Lord’s husbandry (1 Cor 3:9), to remain embracing the divine love that dwells in her.

And perhaps it is also the voice of the Church directed to the community of the Jews, “the daughters of Jerusalem,” who saw the Messiah sleeping on the Cross, buried in the tomb, that they not be disturbed by this and deny faith in Him, for although He appeared as though in weakness, He rises when He pleases, on the third day. He slept on the Cross by His will, and rises also by His will, for He says:
“I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again,” but alas, the Jews refused to accept the crucified Lord Christ, awaiting a messiah according to the desires of their hearts.

entries.section: The suitor seeks his betrothed

paragraphs.text: 1. He comes down to her Himself. 2. He warns her of the slanderers. 3. The wedding banquet.

entries.section: He comes down to her Himself

paragraphs.text: “The voice of my beloved (my sister’s son)! behold, he cometh triumphant upon the mountains, leaping upon the hills. My beloved (my sister’s son) is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, flashing through the lattices” [8-9].

The Church of the Gentiles speaks with the Jewish people in gentle reproach, saying to them: I have come to know “the Word of God,” or the voice of the Beloved, who came incarnate through the Jews (my sister’s son); I knew Him through the mountains of the Law that you received and the hills of the prophecies that are in your hands. He came to me triumphantly with joy and gladness through the Law and the prophecies, but in the fullness of time He came to me Himself like the roe, carrying our nature, hiding behind it—standing behind our wall—speaking with us directly.
I received the message of His Incarnation through the windows of the Law and the lattices of the prophets... I knew His voice and was able to distinguish it (Jn 10:3-4).

In this St. Gregory of Nyssa says: [The brightness (of the Word) reached the Church by way of the prophets first. Finally, by the proclamation of the Gospel the shadows of the types vanished completely and the dividing wall was torn down, and the atmosphere of the inner house was joined to the light of the heights of heaven; there was no more need for the light of the windows since the true light had illumined all the inside with the rays of the Gospel].

entries.section: A meeting on the mountains:

paragraphs.text: If the Church had come to know the incarnate Word of God through the law of the Old Testament and the prophecies, the speech here comes as a call directed to every soul to rise by the Holy Spirit upon the mountains of Holy Scripture to meet there the Suitor who comes to betroth His betrothed. Therefore the psalmist says: “His foundation is in the holy mountains,” “I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help” (Ps 86:1; 120:1).

Origen sees that the soul that wants to meet with “the Word of God,” who is triumphant on the mountains, leaping on the hills in perfect freedom, must meet Him on the bare mountains of the books of the New Testament and upon the hills of the books of the Old Testament which remained for a long time hidden and not perceived.

In the book of Jeremiah we find the Lord sending hunters and fishers to catch men on every mountain and upon every hill (Jer 16:16), as though it were a prophecy of the preaching work of the Church, where the Church catches souls through Holy Scripture to enjoy the blessings of salvation.

On these holy mountains souls meet the Word of God, and see Him as the Suitor who asks for her hand. There she hears the voice of His call to her, so she experiences His love and His divine mysteries are unveiled and she beholds His glory.

As though the soul rises with Moses the prophet on Mount Horeb and sees the bush burning with fire and not consumed (Ex 3:2), she perceives the mystery of the divine Incarnation, as she sees the Virgin Mary (the bush) bearing the coal of divinity and not consumed...
I say that she also ascends with Moses on the mountain to receive the divine Law, not engraved on two tablets of stone, but with the Word of God Himself dwelling in her heart!

Or as though she sits with the crowds to see her Jesus ascending the mountain, opening His mouth and speaking with her directly and without barriers (Mt 5:1), or she ascends with Him on Mount Tabor that He may be transfigured before her and she perceives the brightness of His divinity and hears Him speak with Moses and Elijah about the matters concerning the events of her salvation. Or as though she climbs with “the Word of God” on the mount of temptation, to see Him tempted and conquering for her sake!

By this the believing soul understands why the Lord Christ called Himself the stone cut out of the mountain without hands, which became a great mountain (Dan 2:43), and why the Church also was called Mount Zion, as an indication of the dwelling of God who dwells on high with His people. She listens to the saying of the two angels to Lot: “Escape for thy life... escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed” (Gen 19:17).

entries.section: She likens Him to the roe and the young harts:

paragraphs.text: To what does the bride liken her betrothed?

“My beloved (my sister’s son) is like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Beth-el” [9]. 1. The Lord Christ is likened to the roe (the gazelle), and the word “roe” in Hebrew means “beauty,” for the Lord Christ came seeking the hand of humanity which sin had corrupted and disfigured in its inner nature and spiritual beauty, to be united with it and pour His beauty upon it. And the Lord summarized this wonderful saving work in a speech of reproach to humanity, in which He said: “And I passed by thee, and saw thee trodden in thine own blood, and I said unto thee, In thy blood live.... I have caused thee to multiply as the bud of the field, and thou hast increased and waxen great, and thou art come to excellent ornaments: thy breasts are fashioned, and thine hair is grown, whereas thou wast naked and bare. Now when I passed by thee, and looked upon thee, behold, thy time was the time of love; and I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness: yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine. Then washed I thee with water; yea, I throughly washed away thy blood from thee, and I anointed thee with oil. I clothed thee also with broidered work, and shod thee with badgers’ skin, and I girded thee about with fine linen, and I covered thee with silk. I decked thee also with ornaments, and I put bracelets upon thy hands, and a chain on thy neck. And I put a ring in thy nose, and earrings in thine ears, and a beautiful crown upon thine head. Thus wast thou decked with gold and silver; and thy raiment was of fine linen, and silk, and broidered work; thou didst eat fine flour, and honey, and oil: and thou wast exceeding beautiful, and thou didst prosper into a kingdom. And thy renown went forth among the heathen for thy beauty: for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee, saith the Lord GOD” (Ezek 16:6-14).

Truly how wonderful is the speech of the Lord the Savior toward the Church whom He joined to Himself after He passed by her and found her cast on the road naked and trodden in her blood, so He sanctified her completely. He spread His skirt over her, that is, He betrothed her as a bride to Himself, and covered her shame and nakedness with His blood, washed her with the water of Baptism and anointed her with the oil of the Myron, and clothed her with His life, and gave her His Gospel, the mystery of her salvation, adorned her with the works of the Holy Spirit, and placed His holy yoke as a collar on her neck, and spread His sweet fragrance that her nose smells, and sanctified her ears and adorned them by hearing the divine promises and the heavenly hymns, and satisfied her with the heavenly Bread, and in short made her “exceeding beautiful,” so she deserved to be a queen, reflecting the splendor of the Savior in her life.
In this St. John Chrysostom says:
[As I said, that He who is great and mighty desired a harlot, and I am speaking of human nature under that name: (harlot).

If a man desires a harlot he is condemned; how then does God desire a harlot to be a bridegroom to her?! What does He do? He did not send to her one of His servants, not an angel nor an archangel nor cherubim nor seraphim, but came down Himself, He who loves her, drawing near to her... He does not lead her as a harlot to the heights, for He does not want to bring a harlot into heaven, but He Himself came down to her. So as long as she is unable to ascend to the heights, He came down on the earth. He came to the harlot and was not ashamed to take hold of her while she was in her drunkenness...].

In other words, the Lord came to us “as a roe” to make of us a beautiful and perfect doe able to live on the heights (the heavenly places), as the psalmist says: “who perfecteth my feet like hinds’ feet, and setteth me upon high places.” 2. And St. Augustine comments on this, saying: [He makes my love perfect, so that it rises above the nets of this world full of thorns and darkness. He sets me upon the high places, and fixes my aim toward the heavenly dwelling that I may be filled with the fulness of God (Eph 3:19)]. 3. Origen sees that the word “roe” in Greek came from the sharpness of its sight, and he comments on that, saying: [And who can see as Christ sees? For He alone sees the Father or knows Him. For although it is said of the pure in heart that they see God, yet they see Him through the revelation of Christ to them (Jn 6:6; Mt 5:8). For it is of the nature of the roe not only to see and perceive accurately but also to give others the ability to see... Therefore Christ is compared to the roe or the gazelle, since He not only sees the Father but makes Him visible to those to whom He gives healing of their sight. But it is fitting for you not to take the speech about “seeing the Father” in any bodily understanding, or suppose that God is as it were visible. For God is not seen by bodily sight, but by the sight of the mind and the spirit... Finally, He gives those to whom He gives the power of seeing God the spirit of knowledge and the spirit of wisdom, so that by this Spirit they behold God; therefore He told His disciples: “he that hath seen me hath seen the Father” (Jn 14:9)]. 4. The roe and the hart are known for swiftness of foot (2 Sam 2:18; 1 Kgs 12:8), for the incarnate Word of God, although He came to us in the last times, that is, thousands of years after the fall, yet this does not mean that God was slow in our salvation... but He was hastening to prepare salvation, running toward us until He came down to us in the fullness of time; He hastened to us before we sought Him or searched for Him. 5. St. Augustine sees in the hart not only swiftness of movement with all its energies, but that in its running it thirsts and so runs toward the water brooks. And on the way it kills snakes and so its thirst for the water brooks increases more than before. Therefore the psalmist says: “As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God” (Ps 42:1).

If the believers gather together in one spirit like one hart longing for the water brooks of the love of God, then the Son of God truly came to us like the hart, thirsting for “our love”... and on the way of our salvation He shattered the old serpent, the devil, because of His love in us. 6. It is of the habits of the hart to leap on the rocks (2 Sam 22:34; Hab 3:19), for the Suitor who came to us did not seek the easy way but hastened to the sufferings with joy for our salvation. And as the Apostle Paul says: “Looking unto the author and finisher of our faith... who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame” (Heb 12:2). 7. According to the Mosaic law, the roe and the hart were among the holy animals, whose eating was permitted (Deut 12:22; 14:5)... Therefore the likeness to the roe and the hart was chosen, because the Suitor, as He stretches out His hand to His bride, offers His most holy Body and Blood as a dowry for her, the mystery of her sanctification and her eternity! 8. As the Suitor was likened to the hart, so His betrothed who carried His features was likened also to the hart, for it is said of her in the book of Psalms: “The voice of the LORD perfecteth the harts and discovereth the rough places” (Ps 29:9). And in the speech of the Lord with Job in the tempest through the cloud He said to him: “Knowest thou the time when the wild goats of the rock bring forth? or canst thou mark when the hinds do calve (the travail of the harts)? Canst thou number the months that they fulfil? or knowest thou the time when they bring forth? They bow themselves, they bring forth their young ones (give birth), they cast out their sorrows (their travail). Their young ones are in good liking, they grow up in the wilderness; they go forth, and return not unto them” (Job 39:1).

Origen comments on the two preceding texts, saying: [Since the speech here is about spiritual harts, the “voice of the LORD,” who is Christ the Word of God, is the One who gives the harts the life of perfection (Ps 29:9)... He is the secret of her perfection. As for the Lord’s speech with Job concerning the harts, here the Lord affirms His personal care for the souls of the believers; He cares for the months of their spiritual pregnancy, and when they give birth to virtues, and cares for her young, raises them and feeds them... as though God, who in the Song of Songs was likened to the hart, in His turn likens us to the hart and to our inner life and our virtues, that is, our conduct in Christ Jesus.

And in the book of Proverbs the wife is likened to the hart and her children to the wild goat... as an image of the Church, the true bride, the wife who loves the Lord her Bridegroom and is full of grace... Therefore it was said: “Let her be unto thee a loving hind and a graceful wild goat” (Prov 5:19). 9. As for His likeness to the young harts, it is an affirmation of the Incarnation, for the unlimited God became a child by His Incarnation, emptying Himself of everything for our sake. 10. His likeness to the hart reminds us of what came as the title of the twenty-second psalm, “To the chief musician upon the hind of the morning,” the psalm that describes the events of the Crucifixion and the Resurrection in some detail; and what is meant by the hind of the morning but the new life that the Savior (who is like the hart) presented to us by His Resurrection on the morning of Sunday?!

And He came triumphant on the mountains, leaping on the hills, to bring His betrothed into the power of the Resurrection, that is, to receive the new life that became hers in Christ Jesus, and as the Apostle Paul says: “raised us up together with him in the heavenly places” (Eph 2:6). 11. Finally, His mention of “the mountains of Beth-el” refers to the Holy Scriptures that belong to the house of God (El), that is, the Church, for we cannot experience the beauty of the Lord nor receive His Incarnation and Resurrection and His work in us except through the Church (the house of God)!

entries.section: His standing behind our wall:

paragraphs.text: 1. When the Savior came down to us seeking us as a bride for Himself, He came to us from heaven and came down even to our wall that we built by our disobedience to God. He came to the veil that separated us from the Holy of Holies of God and stood behind it working and striving unto blood, and shattered it, and opened for us a heavenly way in which we walk.

We built the veil, so we became unable to ascend to Him; therefore He came down to us, and on the Cross the veil of the temple was torn, that He may shine upon us by His Resurrection through the windows and lattices that He made Himself. 2. And “our wall” also refers to our human nature, for He came down to us hidden behind our humanity so that we would not be terrified of Him or fear Him, but accept Him and love union with Him.

entries.section: A call to the Resurrection:

paragraphs.text: The Suitor came down to the house of His betrothed knowing that many nets and snares had been set for her that make her unable to go out of her house alone and rise to His house... He Himself came down, He alone whom the snares of sin cannot hold nor the nets of death catch, for He trod sin under His feet and by His life-giving death trampled death and shattered it in its own home... And now He calls His betrothed to come out with Him and not fear, that she may experience “the risen life” or the new life that has become hers through His Resurrection... saying to her “Rise up, my neighbor” (Song 2:10), do not fear. Trust, I have overcome the world and all its evils and death with all its authority.

Origen comments on the call of Christ to His betrothed, saying: [He says this to her to show her how fitting it is for her to despise the nets that the enemy set in the way, and not to fear the snares when she sees them torn by Him].
He calls her with authority to rise to cleave to Him and become His gentle dove, bearing the fruits of the Resurrection in her life, saying to her:
“Rise up, my neighbor, my fair one, my dove, and come away.
For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone.
The flowers appear on the earth; the time of pruning is come, and the voice of the Turtle-dove is heard in our land.
The fig tree putteth forth her green figs, and the vines with the tender grape give forth their smell” [10-13].

It is a call to the first resurrection, the resurrection of the human soul in Christ Jesus from the death of sin and its rising above bodily sensations and earthly lusts, so that she lives according to the Spirit and not the flesh.

Origen comments on this text, saying: [The Word of God is speaking just now with the beautiful noble soul, to whom He appears through her bodily senses—that is, through her reading Holy Scripture and her listening to teaching—as from windows, through which (the Word of God) appears as a tall and great person speaking to her the preceding words, and bending toward her calls her to rise and go out of the realm of the bodily senses, and cease to remain within the realm of the body, so she deserves to hear the voice: “Ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Rom 8:9).

The Word of God would not have called her His neighbor and united with her and become one spirit with her (1 Cor 6:17), nor called her beautiful, had He not seen her image renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16). And He would not have seen her able to receive the Holy Spirit who descended on Jesus at the Jordan in the form of a dove (Mt 3:6), nor called her “His dove,” had she not perceived the love of the Word of God and longed to go forth to Him swiftly while saying: “Oh that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest” (Ps 55:6). I fly with my affections, I fly with my spiritual perceptions, and I rest when I perceive the treasures of His wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3).

It seems to me that just as those who receive the death of Christ and mortify their members which are upon the earth become partakers in the likeness of His death (Col 3:5; Rom 6:5), so also those who receive the power of the Holy Spirit and are sanctified by Him and are filled with His gifts become doves, in His likeness as He appeared in the form of a dove. They are lifted by the two wings of the Holy Spirit and fly, released from earthly and sensible things to the heavenly places.

And to show that the time has become suitable for the realization of these things, He intervenes in a logical way, saying: “For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone.” For the soul does not become one with the Word of God and unite with Him unless such a time passes, that is, every winter of her personal disturbances and the storms of her vices pass away, so that she is no longer shaken nor “carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14). When all these things pass from the soul, and the storms of lusts flee from her, the flowers of the virtues can begin to appear within her, and the time of pruning comes... Then also “the voice of the turtle-dove” is heard, which certainly refers to the wisdom that the one delegated by the “Word” speaks among the perfect, “the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom” (1 Cor 2:6).

And the mention of the Turtle-dove points to this fact: this bird spends its life in the most hidden and remote places away from the crowds. It loves the mountainous deserts or the hidden regions in the forests, and is always found far from the multitudes, a stranger to the crowds.
And what else suits this time and its delights?

He says: “The fig tree putteth forth her green figs,” for the spiritual man whom the fig tree signifies has not yet borne the fruits of the Spirit: love, joy, peace and the rest of these things (Gal 5:22), but has now begun to bear the unripe figs (the small buds).

Truly the trees in their various kinds are understood in the Church generally as a symbol of the souls of the believers, for it was written of them: “Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up” (Mt 15:13). And also Paul, who calls himself “a labourer together with God” in His vineyard (1 Cor 3:9), says: “I have planted, Apollos watered” (1 Cor 3:6). And the Lord Himself says in the Gospel: “Make the tree good, and his fruit good” (Mt 12:33). Thus since the trees in their various kinds are understood in the Church as the souls of the believers, the multiplicity of their kinds symbolizes the different powers and varied virtues of these souls.

Therefore there is in the soul the fig tree that brings forth its green figs, as there is the vine that brings forth its tender grapes and gives forth its sweet smell. And the Husbandman is the heavenly Father, who prunes the vine that it may bring forth more fruit (Jn 15:1)....

And the wonder is that while He calls her to the experience of the Resurrection, saying to her “Rise up,” He says to her “the time of pruning is come,” that is, the time of pruning the vineyard, which refers to crucifixion and suffering... where He removes from her the branches of the works of her old man and the temporal carnal thoughts so that she may bring forth more spiritual fruit bearing heavenly marks! He brings her into sufferings and the Cross that she may bear the fruit of the Resurrection. He separates her from the winter of the biting coldness of the spirit to bring her into the spring of the new risen life in Christ Jesus.

We can also see this call to the Resurrection directed to the whole world... to Jews and Gentiles, for the fig tree refers to the Law, so that by the descent of the Word to the world the Law is no longer understood through the killing letter but we were given to understand it spiritually...

So the Jews who accepted the Lord Christ bore the fruit of the Spirit and their hearts were enlarged with love toward all humanity. The Law was no longer for them a cause of pride and arrogance over the Gentiles as they had been before... therefore He says “the fig tree putteth forth her green figs.” And He also says: “the time of pruning is come,” that is, pruning of the vine, for if the vine referred in the Old Testament to the Jewish people, then its arrogant branches must be pruned so that it may receive the membership of the community of the Gentiles with it, and the sweet fragrance of Christ spreads to fill the whole world. The vine must be pruned of temporal earthly concepts that it may have spiritual heavenly perceptions.

entries.section: The Resurrection: going out from coldness to warmth:

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that this spring in which the flowers appeared and the fig tree put forth its green figs and the fragrance of the vine blossoms spread is the work of God, as the psalmist says: “The summer and the spring thou hast made them” (Ps 73:17). The winter of biting cold had ended and spring came with its warmth. In the winter man was in the coldness of idolatry; his changing nature had turned into the nature of the inanimate things he worshiped. For just as those who look to the true God receive the characteristics of the divine nature within them, so those who look to the vanity of idols are turned themselves into the very things they look at, becoming stones, not men. By worshiping idols they became immobile stone unable to progress... Therefore “the Sun of Righteousness” rose in this biting winter and spring came. The south wind removed this stiffness, and with the appearance of the rays of the sun warmth prevailed over everything on which the rays fell...

If the pagan cold of winter turned man into stone, then the divine Word, "the Sun of Righteousness", has risen, turning the frozen stone into warm waters, as the psalmist says: "Which turned the rock into a standing water, the flint into a fountain of waters". He has raised up children to Abraham from stones (Mt 3:9).

In this spring which the Lord made (by His resurrection), the divine Word calls His bride to arise, saying to her: "Arise, my near one, my fair one, my dove, and come away" [10]. Here the call is directed to the bride to arise and to advance in the way of perfection, just as the Lord said to the paralytic: "Arise, take up thy bed, and walk" (Mt 9:6). The Word did not ask him only to take up his bed but commanded him to walk, and I think that by walking He meant here advancement and growth in perfection. Here too He commands His bride: "Arise, and come away"... This command carries a power which the Bridegroom gives His bride to arise and to walk in the way of perfection.

As for His calling her "my near one, my fair one, my dove," the words came in a precise order, and as St. Gregory says: [Observe the order of the words, how each word is connected with the one before it. See how the thought came linked together as in a chain. The bride hears the commandment, and it carries the power of accomplishment by the Word: she arises, then she advances, and becomes fair, then she is called a dove. For how can you see a beautiful image in a mirror unless the mirror receives the reflection of a beautiful form?! So also with the mirror of human nature: it cannot become beautiful unless the Beautiful One (God) draws near to it, and it is formed by the image of the divine beauty. When our human nature fell to the earth and looked upon the serpent, it bore its image. And now it arises and looks upon the Good, turning its back to sin, and bears the image of the Good which it faces, as it now looks at the original beauty, that is, the dove. As it turns toward the light, it bears the image of the light, and through this light it bears the form of the beloved dove, I mean the dove that symbolized the presence of the Holy Spirit].

This is the secret of bearing fruit in the spring: by His resurrection He drew near to us and we drew near to Him (my near one), and we bore His beauty within us (my fair one), so we became His dove (since the Holy Spirit dwelt in our inner life).

entries.section: Repetition of the call to resurrection:

paragraphs.text: The Lord repeats the call to His betrothed to arise, saying to her:
"Arise, and come away, my near one, my fair one, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the covert of the strongholds.
Let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely" [13-14].

Why does the Suitor repeat the call to His bride to arise? St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, answers, saying: [He calls the bride who has arisen to arise again, and her who has drawn near to Him to come to Him... for it is fitting for her to go from glory to glory (2 Cor 3:18), and she is always looking at what she is, so she sees herself as far less than she wishes to be. So although she is a "dove" by her perfection in Christ, He commands her again to become a "dove," that is, to enter into a more perfect state, and while she is standing, He calls her to arise, giving her power to arise continually and for a life of growth and progress.

The first time He calls her to arise and come to Him: "Arise... and come away"; but now He calls her to go out from her house and from her city and to set out to the clefts of the rock, to the covert of the strongholds. For since the time of winter, in which the bride had shut herself in, has passed, she must now go out and depart, not only from the evil lusts of the flesh but from the whole visible world... He calls her to meet with Him within the eternal, invisible fortresses!

If the Apostle saw in the rock which followed the people of old the person of Christ Himself (1 Cor 10:4), then the Bridegroom here asks His bride not only to go out from herself and from the visible world but rather to enter into Christ Himself, the true Rock, so that she may live with Him without veil or covering... but she beholds His glory with open face (2 Cor 3:18), and speaks with Him.

Her entering the rock to meet with the Bridegroom indicates her security, for there the ancient serpent cannot find a path, as it is written in the Book of Proverbs: "There be three things which are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not: the way of an eagle in the air; the way of a serpent upon a rock..." (Prov 30:18). Origen comments on this, saying: [There is no path for the serpent (on the rock), that is, there can be no trace of sin on this rock which is Christ, for He alone is without sin. So when souls benefit from taking refuge within this rock, they go in peace to the place of the strongholds, that is, they enjoy contemplation of eternal, incorporeal things].

David spoke of this rock in another figurative way in the Psalm: "He set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings" (Ps 40:3). Do not wonder if the rock is for David like ground or a foundation on which the soul walks toward God, while for Solomon it is the covering set over the soul so that it may enjoy the inner mysteries of wisdom, for the Lord Christ Himself was once called the Way (Jn 14:6) in which the believers walk, and at another time He was called the Forerunner, as Paul says: "Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus" (Heb 6:20).

In the same way came God's word to Moses: "I will put thee in a clift of the rock... and thou shalt see my back parts" (Ex 23:22-23). This rock is Christ; it was not completely closed but had a cleft, and (at the same time) this cleft of the rock is also He who reveals God to men and makes Him known to them, since no man knows the Father save the Son (Mt 11:27). No one sees the back parts of God, that is, the things that happen in the last times, unless he enters into the cleft which is in the rock, that is, learns them through the revelation of Christ Himself.
Therefore Christ's call to the soul to arise is a call to enter into Christ Jesus so as to meet with God with open face... "Let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice."

This saying does not mean that her face is hidden from Him or her voice unknown to Him, but He wants her to enter into union with Him, so that she appears before Him with the boldness of love as a bride who appears without a mask, and speaks in complete frankness.!
Origen comments on this call, saying:

[Here under the covering of the rock the Word of God calls the soul that has become His near one to enter into the strongholds, which, as we have said before, means contemplation of the eternal, invisible things. There He says to her: "Let me see thy countenance." For surely there is no longer any trace of the old veil that was upon her face, but she has come to contemplate the glory of God without fear, saying: "And we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth" (Jn 1:14)].

And when she becomes worthy that what was said of Moses be said of her: "Moses spake, and God answered him" (Ex 19:19), His saying is fulfilled in her: "Let me hear thy voice." Truly, what great praise she enjoys when it is said to her: "Sweet is thy voice!" David, the very wise father, also said so: "My meditation of him shall be sweet" (Ps 104:34). For the voice of the soul is sweet when it speaks the word of God, and expounds the faith and the teachings of truth, and reveals God's dealings and His judgments. But if foolish talk comes out of the mouth, or elegant jesting, or trifles, or idle words for which she will give account in the day of judgment (Mt 12:36), then this voice is neither sweet nor delightful. Christ gives no ear to such a voice! Therefore the perfect soul sets a watch before her mouth and a fortified door upon her lips, so that what she utters may be seasoned with salt, with grace toward those who hear it (Col 4:6), and then the Word of God says: "Sweet is thy voice."

He says also: "And thy countenance is comely." You can discern what kind of "countenance" this is which the Word of God praised and described as comely, if you understand what Paul meant by the countenance when he said: "But we all... with open face beholding" (2 Cor 3:18), and also: "but then face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). It is without doubt a kind of countenance that is renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16), after the image of Him that created it (Col 3:10), having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but holy and without blemish, like the Church which Christ presents to Himself (Eph 5:27); in other words, it means the souls that have attained perfection, those which form the body of the Church. This body truly appears beautiful and comely when the souls of which it is composed persevere in obtaining the beauty of perfection. For just as the soul, when it is agitated, distorts the form of the bodily face and makes it provoking, but when it is calm gives the face a form that carries peace and gentleness, so also the face of the Church is beautiful or ugly according to the character and aspirations of the believers. It is written: "A cheerful countenance is a sign of a heart that is in prosperity" (Sir 13:26), and in another place it is said: "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken" (Prov 15:13). The heart is joyful when the Spirit of God is in it, whose first fruit is love and the second is joy (Gal 5:22). And I think that worldly wisdom took its ideas from these truths when it said that the wise man is beautiful and every wicked man is ugly.

It remains for us to give a lengthy explanation of "the covert of the strongholds." For this expression, as we said before, means the presence of a wall before a wall, and this is what Isaiah expressed: "salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks" (Isa 26:1). The wall signifies the city, and the other wall which is before the first or around it signifies greater and stronger fortifications. And the Word of God calls the soul and leads her out of her bodily concerns and sensory perceptions and brings her out to teach her the mysteries of the other life, so that she is in a fortress, in order that, as she is strengthened and surrounded by hope in the eternal things, no bait draws her away and no trials disturb her.

Thus the call of the Lord Christ to the Church or to the human soul for the experience of resurrection is a call to set out from the human self and to depart from bodily things, and to cross over to the new heavenly life... It is an entrance into "the covert of the strongholds," that is, into the bosom of the heavenly Father in which the Church is fortified as the dove of Christ. Thus Christ who rose from the dead wants to enter with His believers into the bosom of His Father and to reveal to them the divine mysteries, as He says to them: "No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him" (Jn 1:18). Again He says: "for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you" (Jn 15:15), and also: "Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me" (Jn 17:24).

He calls her to union with Him, "the true Rock," and to enter with Him into the bosom of His Father, "the covert of the strongholds," to be with Him forever... These are the eternal fortresses which bestow beauty on the Church, so that her voice is sweet and her countenance comely.!

Thus the Suitor calls His betrothed to fly from the realm of carnal thought to spiritual thought, so that she may no longer be "a silly dove" (Hos 7:11) but He sees her meek and pure, and longs for her prayers and her clinging to Him... He sees her face continually and hears her voice.

entries.section: He warns her against the slanderers

paragraphs.text: If the "Word of God" has come down to man, stretching out His hand to him, and man has received Him, He returns to warn him against the slanderers, who work to destroy the union of God with the believing man, saying:
"Take (seize) us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines have tender grapes (have blossomed)" [15].

In His repeating the word "foxes" there is a warning against them, for they creep lightly and enter through small holes to spoil the vineyard at the beginning of its growth... By this they spoil huge quantities of the coming fruit; although they are small, they spoil man's growth and maturity.

entries.section: What are these little foxes?

paragraphs.text: 1. If we take this warning as directed from the Lord Christ to the believer or to the soul that is joined to her Christ, then these little foxes may be sins which we consider slight, such as the white lie or jesting... They may be witty friends or certain books or a certain place... Therefore it is fitting for us to keep all our inner doors closed against any little fox, abstaining from all appearance of evil (1 Thess 5:22).

Origen sees that these little foxes [are the opposing powers of the demons which destroy the flowers of the virtues in the soul and scatter the fruit of faith through the corrupt thoughts and misleading notions which they instill]. He also says: [Surely at the moment of sin, some evil spirit is present in the heart of man, and there he works. We allow him to enter and receive him within us by our evil inclinations].

And as St. Mark the Ascetic says: [Satan offers us small sins that seem trivial in our eyes, because without this he cannot lead us to great sins]. 2. If we take this warning as directed from the Lord Christ to the Church, Origen says: [These words appear to be directed to the teachers of the Church, so the commands are given them to catch the foxes that spoil the vines. Here the foxes are understood as the teachers who promote heretical doctrines, those who mislead the hearts of the simple and spoil the vineyard of the Lord so that it does not bring forth the blossom of Orthodox faith, using their embellished arguments. Therefore the commands are given to the teachers of the Catholic Church to hasten to rebuke these foxes and resist them while they are still small and beginners in their corrupt teachings, and to subdue the opponents of the word of truth and take them captive by showing the truth].

entries.section: The little foxes in the Holy Bible:

paragraphs.text: It is written in the Book of Psalms: "But those that seek my soul, to destroy it, shall go into the lower parts of the earth. They shall fall by the sword: they shall be a portion for foxes (jackals)" (Ps 63:9-10). These are the wicked teachers who wish to deceive the soul, so they push it to destruction with vain embellished words; they use earthly, temporal wisdom, so they take the souls of the righteous into the lower parts of the earth instead of lifting them up toward the eternal and heavenly things, and they make their own souls and the souls of those whom they teach a portion for the foxes (evil teachings or demons) instead of being the portion of the Lord. To such as these the Lord says: "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head" (Mt 8:20). The Lord finds no place in their hearts to rest, but the demons (the foxes) rest, and their souls turn into dens for them.
Since Herod became misleading, the Lord also called him a fox (Lk 13:31).

And in the Book of Judges we find Samson who caught three hundred foxes and took firebrands and turned tail to tail and put a firebrand in the midst between every two tails; then he set the brands on fire and let them go into the standing corn of the foreign pagans, and burnt up both the shocks and the standing corn, with the olive yards (Judg 15:3-5). He represents the true and faithful teacher who knows how to gather all the heresies and tie their tails together, showing the heresies' opposition to one another, and when he kindles in them the fire of truth, the fields of evil, innovations and heresies are burnt up.

And in the Book of Nehemiah Tobiah the Ammonite stands mocking what Nehemiah was doing, saying: "Even that which they build, if a fox go up, he shall even break down their stone wall" (Neh 4:3). This is a symbolic picture of what the world does when it sees the walls of the Gospel raised up with the believers, the living stones who have gone out from the captivity of sin to become a wall and a temple at a heavenly level. The world mocks, saying that the Gospel was not established on earthly philosophical foundations, supposing that any fox or earthly argument is able to demolish it.!

The Holy Bible has taught us to beware of the little foxes but not to fear them, for we have been given power to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy (Lk 10:19)... We say in Christ Jesus: "Happy shall he be, that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones" (Ps 137:9), the Rock. For we strive to destroy evil from the beginning of its going forth and to bury it under the feet of Christ our Rock.

entries.section: The hunters of the little foxes:

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, sees that the hunters of the little foxes are the angelic powers or the company of the holy Apostles: 1. Perhaps they are the angelic powers who accompany the Lord in His descent to earth and work for the sake of His Kingdom, for it was said of the Lord that He is "strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle" (Ps 24:8). 2. They may represent the Apostles who were sent to hunt such beasts of prey out of the hearts of men, to make a place for the Son of man in which to lay His head.

entries.section: The hunters of the little foxes:

paragraphs.text: By the divine Incarnation the Suitor came down to His betrothed to ask for her hand, and by His resurrection He called her to arise in Him and with Him, so that she does not fear death nor dread the authority of sin, but He asked her to beware of the foxes that spoil the vineyard of union with Him. The bride responded to the repeated call of the Suitor "Arise... come away," so she entered the wedding banquet, which is His crucifixion and resurrection, to enjoy union with Him, and she communed with Him, saying:
"My beloved (my near one) is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies.
Until the day break (breathe), and the shadows flee away, turn, my beloved (my near one), and be thou like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Bether (the narrow mountains)" [16-17].

entries.section: Recognizing the One who rose from the dead:

paragraphs.text: After the bride sang, praising the effectiveness of the Cross in her life and declaring that the banquet of the resurrection is the wedding banquet, during which she enjoys union with the Bridegroom and her inner depths set out toward His final coming, she reviewed, in a symbolic picture, the events of the resurrection as they concern her, and said:

"By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not; I called him, but he gave me no answer. I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not. The watchmen that go about the city found me: to whom I said, Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?

It was but a little that I passed from them, but I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me.
I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds (mighty ones) of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" [1-5].
We can interpret this speech from two points of view: as the speech of the Catholic Church to her Bridegroom Christ, or as the speech of the soul, as a member of the Church, with her Christ.

entries.section: 1. The first interpretation: the speech of the Catholic Church:

paragraphs.text: This symbolic speech carries a living picture of the events of the resurrection as they concern the Church since her Bridegroom was lifted up on the Cross; she sought Him three times and did not find Him except the last time.

a. The first time she sought Him "by night," and perhaps this is a reference to the darkness that covered the earth at the moments of the Cross, for the Scripture says: "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour. And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice... and, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent; and the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose" (Mt 27:45-52).

The day became night, and there was darkness over all the land, and not even the disciples were able to grasp the mystery of salvation at that time... for they had not yet enjoyed the enlightenment. They sought Him on their beds and did not find Him, and they called Him and He did not answer them. They sought Him in the darkness of fleshly human thinking, on their beds, unable to strive with Him or to grasp the mysteries of the Spirit, so they did not find Him. Perhaps they were asking within their thoughts: Is this the Messiah, the Savior?! Or, in the words of the two disciples of Emmaus afterward: "We trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel" (Lk 24:21). Perhaps they expected that He would escape from the hands of those who crucified Him and avenge Himself and establish His kingdom at that time, but nothing of this happened at all!

b. The second time the bride sought Him by night, not on her bed but, as she said: "I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways," and this is a reference to the state of the disciples after the Lord was buried and they entered the upper room and all their time turned into night, for they sought the Lord while afraid, with the doors shut. They tried to regain their strength, and they rose and searched for Him in the city, in the streets and the broad ways. It was the Sabbath, but they did not taste the flavor of rest, nor were they able to be still; rather their upper room, not the city, was turned, and their thoughts and perhaps their conversations together were turned into streets and broad ways, each one asking within himself or with his companions: And what is the end of the matter?! They searched for Him among themselves and were tossed about in their depths, and there was no peace!

c. In the third time the search for Him was accomplished at the empty tomb, for Mary went out at dawn on Sunday while the darkness remained; she did not care to walk in the streets and broad ways until she passed by the tomb. She went out on behalf of the Church with a sorrowful heart and asked the angel with tears about Him whom her soul loved, and she had scarcely passed him when she saw the Lord and clung to Him... She held Him at first, but when she wished to remain so, He asked her to hasten and tell the disciples to meet Him in Galilee... as though St. Mary had brought Him into the Church, the house of her mother and the chamber of her that conceived her.

As for the speech of the Church: "I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds (mighty ones) of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please," it is a speech of reproach filled with love, directed from the Christian Church to the company of the Jews. They mocked the Bridegroom on the Cross, saying: "If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross" (Mt 27:40), and the chief priests also, mocking with the scribes and elders, said: "He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him" (Mt 27:41-42). It is as though the Church, after entering into His resurrection, returned to say to the daughters of Jerusalem: Why were you hastening the Bridegroom to arise? I charge you by the prophets, "the roes and the hinds of the field," to leave Him to arise on the third day wherever He pleases! If He has slept on the Cross, then review the prophecies and remember that He rises when He pleases! I have now come to know the mystery of His death and burial: He died by power, and rose to raise us with Him!

entries.section: 2. The second interpretation: the speech of the human soul:

paragraphs.text: If the Church sought Him three times, while He was on the Cross, while He was in the tomb, and finally after His resurrection at the empty tomb... and on the third day she found Him, then the human soul in her search for Him may seek Him three times or in three ways, but she does not find Him except in the last way: she seeks Him by her own effort, or she seeks Him through the servants alone, and finally she seeks Him with confidence in the possibilities of God's work in her, without ignoring her own striving or the service of the workers in His vineyard.

a. Seeking the Lord by one's own human effort: The soul began her speech: "By night on my bed..." Perhaps in her time of weakness she dreamed a troubling dream that she had lost her Bridegroom, so she went out to search for Him by her own effort, but she cannot meet with Him unless He draws her to Himself.

Perhaps by night she meant that she had become slack in the darkness of recklessness, seeking Him while lying on her bed in idle dependence without true spiritual striving... Therefore she sought Him and did not find Him. She did not rest on the bed which she described before: "our bed is green" (Song 1:16), but she wanted to lie on her own human bed.

We saw that the speech about "our green bed" refers to the union of God the Word with our humanity, as He took our body into Himself, whereas the speech about "my bed" or "my couch" refers to "my body" or "my humanity" in its isolation or its self-reliance. St. Augustine sought the Lord while lying on his couch when he went out to search for Him in pride and did not find Him, for he said: [I shut the door of my God against myself... and when I wished to knock that it might be opened to me, I was working all the more to make it fast shut, because I dared to search in pride for Him whom only the humble know... While I was perishing I thought I was able to fly, so I left the nest and fell before I could fly, but the God of mercy raised me up so that passers-by would not trample me with their feet to death, and He put me in the nest].

St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, sees that she calls Him here "him whom my soul loveth" and does not give Him a name, because when she sought Him by a name, Him who cannot be named, she did not find Him... She asked about Him the angelic powers who were gathered together praising in countless numbers, and they fell silent... for she seeks Him who cannot be comprehended in a limited, comprehending way... and in their silence she realized her error. Therefore she is careful now not to give Him any title.

b. In the second stage the soul went out from herself, for she left her bed saying "I will rise," and entered the city to search for her Bridegroom, searching for Him within the city in the streets and the broad ways.

Augustine went out to the streets and broad ways by searching for God through the books of the philosophers, and in the streets by searching for Him in nature, but he did not find God, for in his foolishness he went out to seek God outside himself, although God was within him, deeper than his depths and higher than his height.

Perhaps the city here refers to the Holy Bible, so the soul entered the streets and broad ways of the Scripture, that is, its symbols and prophecies, and yet she was not able to meet her Bridegroom, because she did not ask for the help of God who draws her to Himself. This is what the chief priests and scribes of the people did when they searched in the Scripture and learned about the Messiah that He would be born in Bethlehem of Judea (Mt 2:4-6), informing Herod of this without themselves meeting their Christ!

c. In the third stage she searched for Him through "the watchmen," who are the servants of the divine Word, and this time also she is not able to meet her Bridegroom except after passing them a little. For the workers in the vineyard support the soul to enter to the Bridegroom, but they cannot bring her in to Him except by His own work, for He alone is able to draw the heart toward Himself.

Truly, the priests are committed to keeping watch, but "Except the LORD keep the city, the watchmen wake but in vain" (Ps 27:1). If they perform the priestly work, it is through the Bridegroom Himself, "a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek."

The Apostle Paul realized his people's obligation to pass beyond him and his companions, for he affirmed to the Corinthians: "Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos?... I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase" (1 Cor 3:5-6).

In Christ Jesus Himself the soul experiences union with Him, so she enters by Him into her depths, into the inner heart; they commune together far from all eyes, revealing their secrets to one another without affectation!

She asks the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, those who are close to her, to leave her with her Bridegroom in a life of stillness and hidden prayer... for she wishes that nothing distract her from remaining in the arms of this life-giving Bridegroom.

entries.section: The risen bride:

paragraphs.text: The troubling dream has ended and the darkness has dispersed by the resurrection of the Lord, so we recognized Him and enjoyed union with Him, and the mark of His "resurrection" became ours. Therefore the angels stood as friends of the Bridegroom who rose from the dead, singing and praising the bride who has risen with her Bridegroom, saying:
"Who is this that cometh out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all powders of the merchant?" [6].

It is noticed that this speech cannot apply to carnal love, otherwise what would be the connection between it and the speech preceding it? For at the beginning of the chapter we see the bride slack on her bed seeking her Bridegroom and not finding Him, and after the effort she met Him and brought Him into her mother's house, and now we suddenly see her described as coming up from the wilderness perfumed with myrrh and frankincense and adorned with all the cosmetics (powders) bought from the merchant... Would she bring Him into her mother's house and leave Him to go out with perfumes and adornment?! But it is a wonderful spiritual speech, for the bride, having met her Bridegroom who rose from the dead and ascended to His heavens, brought Him into her heart... and the natural fruit of this work was that she ascended with Him and by Him to His heavens, as the Apostle Paul says: "hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places." His entering into her depths lifted her above the wilderness of this life, so she communed with Him: "I have a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better" (Phil 1:23).

Perhaps these words "Who is this that cometh up...?" come from the Bridegroom Himself, who supports her and encourages her, assuring her that He sees her ascending to the heavens although she is now on earth. While still in the body she has become like the smoke that carries the fragrance of sweet prayer, in which are the breaths of the Bridegroom Himself. And perhaps they are the words of the heavenly ones who looked upon the earthly human beings, when the door of Paradise was opened before them and they set out with the Lord Christ dwelling in them, rising from day to day toward the heavenly things; and perhaps also the words of the daughters of Jerusalem, those who were formerly reproaching the Church for her blackness, as we saw before, because of her not belonging to the fathers and the prophets... since she is of the Gentiles, but she now appears, through her union with the Messiah the Savior, beautiful and radiant, ascending from glory to glory.!

entries.section: Ascending from the wilderness:

paragraphs.text: In the old days the people of Israel wandered forty years in the wilderness, in which they were exposed to the bites of deadly serpents because of their disobedience and murmuring, and the Gentiles were bound to the wilderness of the world and were defiled with evils... But now the believers have been united with the Messiah, who alone is able to bring man out of the wilderness of this world to the freedom of the heavenly Kingdom, as the Lord Himself says: "And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven" (Jn 3:13). And as St. John Chrysostom says: [We who were formerly unworthy of earthly glory now ascend to the Kingdom of Heaven, and enter the heavens, and take our place before the divine throne].

entries.section: Perfumed pillars of smoke:

paragraphs.text: In the old days God used to descend upon Mount Sinai and it smoked, a sign of the splendor of His glory and His power (Ex 19:18; 20:18; Ps 104:32; 144:5), and when His glory descended in His holy house, whether the Tabernacle or the Temple, the place was filled with smoke (Isa 6:4; cf. Rev 15:8). But now that the heart of the believer has opened to the Lord, his very life has become a glory to God, it has become a sweet smoke ascending from the wilderness of this world and rising toward heaven.

The smoke used to signify God's coming down and His presence to give a promise to His beloved ones, as He did with Abram when he divided the bloody sacrifices in the midst and the Lord entered with him into living promises, for a smoking furnace and a burning lamp passed between the pieces (Gen 15:17); but now the Lord has dwelt in the heart of His people and set out with them like smoke, not that they may hear promises from God but that they may enjoy God Himself, their portion and their inheritance.

The smoke also used to signify the Lord's presence to sanctify His people, as the prophet Isaiah says: "When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall have purged the blood of Jerusalem from the midst thereof by the spirit of judgment, and by the spirit of burning. And the LORD will create upon every dwelling place of mount Zion, and upon her assemblies, a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night" (Isa 4:4-5); but now that the Church has been sanctified in the blood of Christ and washed in the waters of Baptism, the fire of the Holy Spirit has kindled her, so she has become a holy smoke rising to where Christ sits.

The smoke signifies the life of prayer, as St. John the Theologian says: "And the smoke of the incense, which came with the prayers of the saints, ascended up before God out of the angel's hand" (Rev 8:4)... Therefore it is said in the Song of Songs that she who ascends is like pillars of incense, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense... because frankincense is a symbol of the life of prayer.

At any rate, it is not a smoke that fills the world with suffocation, a sign of God's anger (Deut 29:20; Isa 34:10; Rev 9:2; 14:11; 18:9, 18; 19:3), so that she would be like Sodom and Gomorrah where the smoke of the land went up as the smoke of a furnace (Gen 19:28). Nor does it carry the sign of weakness and death, as the prophet says: "the heavens shall vanish away like smoke" (Isa 51:6), and the psalmist's saying: "For my days are consumed in smoke" (Ps 102), nor the sign of the evil and sloth which spoil the inner sight, as the wise man says: "As smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to them that send him" (Prov 10:26).

That smoke chokes the soul and spoils the eyes, but the bride is pillars of perfumed smoke that gladden heaven and delight it, and the materials of her perfume are: 1. Myrrh, because she was buried with Christ Jesus, who was wrapped with myrrh and spices; for if she is not buried with Him she cannot enjoy the new life, risen and lifted toward the heavens, as the Apostle says: "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life" (Rom 6:4). We are buried in Baptism, and our old man dies, and we are born a new, spiritual birth, so that by the Holy Spirit we may be lifted up to our heavenly Father.

On this St. John Chrysostom says: [It is not by a mother and a father, not by the lying down of men, nor by the pains of labor that we are born again, but from the Holy Spirit our new tissues are made, and in the water they are formed, and from the water we are born mystically as from the womb... The womb needs much time for the body to be formed in it, but from the water and the Spirit the life of the Spirit is formed in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye! That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit (Jn 3:6)].

He says also: [When the head is plunged under the water as in a tomb, our whole old humanity is poured out into it... and when you come out after that, it floats and comes out, our man made new. And as it is easy for us to plunge and then to float, so it is easy for God to bury the old humanity and clothe us with the new man]. 2. Frankincense, for the fragrance of the incense of her prayers ascends toward the Lord... and she even repeats with the psalmist: "But I give myself unto prayer." In her union with the One who rose from the dead she comes to know the life of true worship or "unceasing prayer." 3. All the powders of the merchant, which are the cosmetics that the soul buys from Christ Himself, "the Merchant," who alone is able to adorn the soul and beautify her as a bride for Himself.

Thus the soul needs to be perfumed by Baptism and to lean on the Holy Spirit, to live her life as unceasing prayer, and to cast herself into the arms of her Bridegroom that He may adorn her... By this she is worthy to be presented as a bride adorned for her husband (Rev 21:2).
