entries.section: The time of the wedding banquet:

paragraphs.text: "Behold his bed, which is Solomon's; threescore valiant men are about it, of the valiant of Israel. They all hold swords, being expert in war:
every man hath his sword upon his thigh because of fear in the night.
King Solomon made himself a throne of the wood of Lebanon.
He made the pillars thereof of silver, the bottom thereof of gold, the seat of it of purple, the midst thereof being paved with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem" [7-10].

If the Cross of the Lord and His resurrection are the mystery of the wedding banquet, as the Bridegroom who rose from the dead comes forward and raises His bride who entered with Him into the circle of His sufferings and crucifixion, and dwells in her heart so that she ascends by Him to heaven, perfumed and adorned with all spiritual beauty, we ask: When will this be? Or what is the time of the banquet.?

The answer came carrying two aspects: a temporal aspect and an eternal one. We enter into the procession of the Bridegroom and His banquet in the time of our sojourn, in the night of this world, to fight the terrors of the night, striving even to blood, and we enjoy His eternal procession in the day that has no night, where we sit at His right hand, partakers with Him in glory. Therefore the Bridegroom appears in two processions, one in the night where He sets up the bed in the midst of His striving children, and the other in the day, seated on His eternal throne. 1. The temporal procession: In this procession the Bridegroom appears with sixty valiant men around Him, all men of war, carrying their swords upon their thighs, striving amid the terrors of the night of this life. It is the procession that the striving Church lives around Christ her Bridegroom.

Here the Bridegroom appears having set up a "bed" in the midst of the Church, but it is not like the bed of the bride who lay on it in the night (Song 3:1), seeking her Bridegroom in slackness and not finding Him, calling Him and He does not answer her! Nor like the beds into which the frogs came up (Ex 8:3), a sign of God's anger and His plagues on Pharaoh, nor like the beds on which men lie when they give up the spirit and lie without movement (Gen 49:33; 2 Kgs 1:4), nor like the bed which David the psalmist made to swim with tears every night (Ps 6:6); rather it is a unique bed on which "the Lion that came out of the tribe of Judah" couched (cf. Gen 49:9), it is the Cross of the Lord which brought about peace for the Church, for by it heaven was reconciled with earth, and it gave victory and triumph to the Church over the spiritual powers of evil.

"Solomon" set it up to declare that it is the mystery of the Church's peace and the sign of her rest; on it the Apostle Peter rested secretly in the prison and slept without disturbance until the angel came to wake him and bring him out (Acts 12:6-10)... He gives His beloved sleep... that is, peace.!

Our true Solomon set up a bed in the midst of His people so that He may sleep continually within the ship of our life (Mt 8:24; Mk 4:38), so we do not perish, whatever severe disturbances occur in the sea.

And to show that it is the bed of spiritual rest and inner peace without slackness or sloth, the Song of Songs shows us that around it are sixty valiant men, all holding swords and expert in war, every man with his sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night. Around the Cross the striving Church gathers as men of war, so that as He overcame, they also overcome by Him and with Him. Every believer carries upon his thigh his sword, which is the word of God, that he may overcome, as it is written in the Book of Revelation: "And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb (that is, by the Cross), and by the word of their testimony (the word of God); and they loved not their lives unto the death" (Rev 12:11).

Who are the sixty valiant men of the valiant of Israel who surround Him? They are the sons of the Kingdom, the new, spiritual Israel, the chosen ones who accepted the Cross and entered with God into a new covenant. These came to the banquet in the pampering of love but without softness; rather they armed themselves with the sword of the Spirit and the helmet of salvation, striving even to blood against sin without relenting. Therefore the Apostle Paul advises us, saying: "Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might. Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God... Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness; and your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace; above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked. And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God" (Eph 6:10-17).

As for the mystery of their number, 60, we know that the number 12 signifies the Kingdom of God on earth, for St. Augustine says that the Holy Trinity (3) reigns over the four corners of the world (4). Thus the Kingdom of God on earth means 3 x 4 (12). Therefore the tribes of the children of Israel were twelve, and the number of the disciples of the New Testament is twelve, and the number of the gates of Jerusalem is twelve gates. St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, sees that each one of them carried five swords, which are the sanctification of the five senses by Christ Jesus our Lord, so the number is (12 x 5 = 60). It is as though all those who have become members of His Kingdom have had their senses sanctified in perfection in Christ Jesus.

St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, says that the sword of the eye is to look continually toward the Lord, that it may see uprightly and not be defiled by anything; and the sword of hearing is to listen to spiritual things and not to give ear to vanity... and likewise for taste, touch and smell, all this is sanctified by the sword of self-control and contact with the Lord Christ and the breathing of His sweet fragrance... By this man fights all the darkness of sin. 2. The eternal procession: In the temporal procession the Bridegroom appeared on His bed to give His people assurance that He is the mystery of their rest and peace amid their striving in this world or in this temporal life, but in the eternal procession there is no war and no striving, so He appears as a king carried on a throne or a litter borne on arms... He appears on His eternal throne which is borne by the four living creatures (Rev 4).
And what is this throne but the Church herself, within whom the Lord dwells and upon whom He sits enthroned forever, and her marks are:

a. She is united with the Cross of the Lord and has become one with Him, therefore she is described as made of wood. Her suffering and crucifixion with the Lord remains the mystery of her life and her eternal glory, for the Apostle says: "if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together" (Rom 8:17).

b. As for her being of the wood of Lebanon, we have seen that Lebanon is famous for its cedar, known for its uprightness and sweet fragrance; so the Church of Christ, which lived in her sojourn with uprightness, not halting between two ways, God and the world, carries the fragrance of Christ her Bridegroom.

c. Her pillars are of silver, the work of our Solomon Himself. And silver signifies in the Holy Bible the word of God refined seven times, as though the shepherds of the Church and her servants have become pillars in her by their hiding themselves and mingling with the word of God...

d. The golden base signifies that the people, having carried the Lord Christ in their practical life, have become heavenly (gold), living on earth as though they were angels of God. Or, as the Apostle says: "that both they that have wives be as though they had none; and they that weep, as though they wept not; and they that rejoice, as though they rejoiced not; and they that buy, as though they possessed not; and they that use this world, as though they used it not" (1 Cor 7:29-31).
e. The purple seat signifies the nature of the Church as a queen united with the eternal King.
f. Her midst is paved with love for the daughters of Jerusalem, since the Church bears the mark of her Bridegroom, who is love, for the salvation of mankind.

entries.section: An invitation to the banquet:

paragraphs.text: "Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion, and behold king Solomon with the crown wherewith his mother crowned him in the day of his espousals, and in the day of the gladness of his heart" [11].

This is the invitation which the Church directs to the world to enjoy the banquet of the Cross. She asks mankind to go out from itself, from the ego... "Go forth," so that they may be able to enjoy the sight of the true King, "the new Solomon," whom the nation of the Jews crowned with a crown of thorns.
Through spiritual insight the believers see the secret crown of the Crucified One, namely "the forgiveness of our sins and the removal of the curse."
This is the day of His wedding and the day of the gladness of His heart, for He offered His blood as a dowry for His bride!

entries.section: The risen bride

paragraphs.text: If by the divine Incarnation the Word of God came down to us to betroth us as a bride for Himself, and by His crucifixion He held the wedding feast, then by His resurrection He has justified us, so we became the risen bride who is without blemish. Therefore the Bridegroom praises her, seeing in her all beauty, and says to her:
"Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair!" [1].

Through the resurrection He bestowed upon the Church all spiritual beauty and power, of which St. Peter the Apostle speaks, saying: "According as his divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness, through the knowledge of him that hath called us to glory and virtue: whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust" (2 Pet 1:3-4). And the marks of this beauty are: 1. "Thine eyes are doves under thy veil (thy silence)" [1].

St. Abdosius says: [The eyes are beautiful as the eyes of a dove because she is in the likeness of the dove of the Holy Spirit who came down from heaven]. We saw before that the Lord likens His Church to the eyes of a dove, because as she looks continually upon the Holy Spirit, His image shines forth upon her eyes, so she has spiritual insight far from every earthly or carnal impression, and she is simple, seeking nothing but what is of God, loving like the dove, and resting only in the arms of the true Noah, as the dove did which went out from the ark.

As for their being under the veil, it is because the mysteries of the Spirit which the eyes of the Church behold cannot be understood or grasped by the world, so they remain for it as though under a veil!

The literal translation is "in thy silence," for the Church, her insight having been opened to behold the spiritual mysteries of God's love, stands in silence contemplating the surpassing works of God, and as St. John Saba says: [Whoever wishes to speak about the love of God proves his ignorance, because speaking about this divine love is not possible at all.
Wonderful also is love!!
It is the language of the angels, and words find it hard to translate it...!
It is not for us, my Lord, to speak out of what is ours about what is Yours. But You speak in us about Yourself, and about all that is Yours, as it pleases You].

And perhaps He described the eyes as under the veil because the believers, however much they enjoy spiritual insight in this world, it is considered as though under a veil when compared with the vision in the eternal life, for the Apostle says: "For we know in part... for now we see in a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known" (1 Cor 13:9, 12). 2. "Thy hair is as a flock of goats couching on mount Gilead" [1].
If the Lord Christ is the head of the Church, then the Church is the hair surrounding the head, which lives upon it; without the head she is worth nothing and has no existence.
This is the people of Christ: it is like a flock of goats feeding on the high mount Gilead, the mountain of the lofty word of God which sets out with the hearts of the children of God toward heaven.

The higher the flock goes up the mountain, the more man sees it from afar in one unity, so that he cannot distinguish one from another... So when we arise with the Lord and are lifted up above through the word of salvation and enjoy His ecclesiastical care, to live in a heavenly spirit, the spirit of division and schism, whose causes are earthly thinking, the seeking of temporal honor and the love of the world, is removed from us.

When we arise with the Lord we ascend mount Gilead like a flock of goats gathering together on the summits, so that it is seen from afar like smooth, black, shining hair into which no gray enters, for the Lord renews our youth like the eagle's.
As for the description of the flock as couching on the mountain, it means sitting and resting in the word of God without haste, settled under God's care in tranquility.
As for His choosing mount Gilead, it is for many reasons:
a. On mount Gilead God appeared to Laban and warned him, saying: "Take heed that thou speak not to Jacob either good or bad" (Gen 31:24)... So the believer feels assurance; no one can touch him...

b. The slopes of mount Gilead were distinguished by abundance of pasture, so it became a figure of the life of satisfaction, for when the Lord promised His people of old that He would deliver them from violent Babylon and bring them into satisfaction, He said to them: "And I will bring Israel again to his habitation, and he shall feed on Carmel and Bashan, and his soul shall be satisfied upon mount Ephraim and Gilead" (Jer 50:19), and in the Book of Micah it is said: "Let them feed in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old" (Mic 7:14).

c. In ancient times balsam grew in Gilead, known for its fragrant scent, which the ancient poets and historians used to praise at length, and which physicians used for healing wounds and diseases. Therefore it is written in Jeremiah the prophet: "Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? Why then is not the daughter of my people bound up?!" (Jer 8:22). It is as though on mount Gilead the true Physician, Jesus Christ, binds up the wounds of His people and heals their diseases with the balsam of His blood poured out on the Cross.

d. When Gideon entered into war with the army of the Midianites, thirty-two thousand of the people gathered for the war, but the Lord said to Gideon: "Whosoever is fearful and afraid, let him return and depart early from mount Gilead" (Judg 7:3). So God does not care about a great number but seeks striving believers who know neither fear nor terror! This is the true Church of Christ, which has been given power to tread on serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy, living in complete confidence without fear.

entries.section: The risen bride

paragraphs.text: 3. "Thy teeth are like a flock of shorn (sheep) that came up from the washing" [2].
It is fitting for the Church to have teeth, for she has grown and matured and the milk of teaching no longer suffices her, but she seeks its rich food, chewing it and digesting it in her life.

St. Augustine says that the teeth of the Church are her servants, who chew the food like nursing mothers and present it as milk to the little ones in the faith. These teeth are of different kinds, canines and molars... but they work for one end and in one spirit for edification.

With these teeth the Lord asked the Apostle Peter to eat the animals after they were slain, and not to call anything unclean or common. For the Church works continually, through her servants, to present the word of salvation to all, slaying the uncleanness of evil and chewing the pagan Gentiles and tearing apart their evil and errors until they become members of her body.

The servant is like the shorn sheep, whose wool is cut... that is, he cuts off from himself the thoughts and works of the flesh by the Holy Spirit who was given to him in the font of Baptism (the washing). For wool in the Holy Bible signifies the carnal life, therefore in the Old Testament the priests were forbidden to enter the sanctuary in garments made of wool, but their garments were to be of linen, a sign of the righteousness of Christ. As the Mosaic Law affirmed: "Thou shalt not wear a garment of divers sorts, as of woollen and linen together" (Deut 23:11), "for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?!" (2 Cor 6:14-15).

entries.section: 4. "Whereof every one beareth twins, and none is barren among them" [2].

paragraphs.text: In the natural child the teeth usually grow in the gums in pairs, and so God used to send His disciples, the teeth of the Church, two by two to preach, perhaps so that one may utter the word of preaching while the other prays for him, so that the word goes forth anointed with divine grace.
When St. Pachomius was asked why he allowed the monks to live in their cells two by two, he answered: because if one falls the other raises him up.

St. Augustine sees in the phrase "beareth twins" a reference to the two commandments that complete each other, "love of God" and "love of neighbor," for by them the Law and the Prophets are fulfilled (Mt 22:40). Meanwhile St. Cyril of Jerusalem sees that it refers to the double grace, that is, that man is perfected by water and the Spirit, or through the graces to which the two Testaments, the Old and the New, pointed.

St. Jerome comments on this phrase, saying: [If none among them is barren, then all must have breasts filled with milk, able to say with the Apostle: "My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you" (Gal 4:19), "I have fed you with milk, and not with meat" (1 Cor 3:2).

Finally we can say that whoever has enjoyed the word of salvation by way of the pure teeth of the Church, that is, her true servants, must not remain barren but bear more than one, that is, have double fruit. Let him imitate the Samaritan woman, who, when she heard the voice of the Lord and met with Him inwardly, called the city of Samaria that they might meet with Him as she did, and Levi also, who gathered his colleagues to enjoy the Savior.

entries.section: 5. "Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet, and thy mouth is sweet" [3].

paragraphs.text: If all the members of the Church are committed to double fruit, then the secret of this is "the lips like a thread of scarlet and the sweet mouth," that is, the believer is committed to bearing witness to the Savior through his lips and his mouth... and the meanings of these lips and this mouth are:

a. In the old days Rahab the harlot tied a cord of scarlet in the window as a sign of her faith in the Lord the Savior and her taking refuge in His blood that forgives sins and her confession of His ownership over her and her house, so she was rescued, she and all who were inside her house, from destruction. This is a living picture of the believer who ties everything that comes out of his mouth to the precious Blood, witnessing for the Lord by his words as by his works, so that he brings all into the house of God and saves all from destruction.

b. When the soldiers wished to mock the Lord they clothed Him with a scarlet robe, the sign of a king. But the Church, having been united with the King, her lips have become like a thread of scarlet; nothing comes out of them that is unbecoming to her as a queen or a bride of the heavenly King.
c. The lips of the bride are like a fine thread, which makes her mouth sweet; no wounding word comes out of it, it does not deceive nor flatter, but is gentle with all and loves everyone.

entries.section: 6. "Thy cheek is like a piece of a pomegranate under thy veil" [3].

paragraphs.text: The garment of the high priest and his ephod were adorned with embroidered pomegranates (Ex 28:33-34; 39:24-26), and the Temple was adorned in various places with carvings in the shape of pomegranates (1 Kgs 7:18). So the pomegranate signifies adornment, with which the Church is beautified as the garment of the Lord Christ, the great High Priest, and the Temple in which His Holy Spirit dwells.

He assigned the pomegranate to the cheek because the cheek signifies the features of man, on which appear the signs of joy or sorrow, peace or distress; and the features of the Church are beautiful, gladdening and filled with peace.

He did not say "thy cheek is like a pomegranate" but "like a piece of a pomegranate," in order to show what is within it, for it is rich in seeds packed with sweet red juice, ever fresh, knowing no withering.!

Her cheek is like a piece of a pomegranate, filled with redness; the secret of her beauty is the blood of the Lord Christ which sanctifies her, so that there is no trace of defilement within her. This redness also signifies the soul's modesty and shame, for she does not conform to the people of this world in arrogance and brazenness of face.
As for her cheek being "under her veil," its secret is not shame before men, but the declaration of the truth of her glory that it is from within (Ps 45).

entries.section: All of them shields of mighty men" [4].

paragraphs.text: The Lord often links the beauty of the Church with her striving, so that the believers understand that their beauty in Christ Jesus has as its secret also their lawful spiritual striving; so the cheek of the Church does not remain beautiful like a piece of a pomegranate without the neck set upright like the tower of David builded for an armoury, that is, without the living, upright, undeviating faith joined with striving.

Through this neck, which is faith, the face of the Church is lifted up to heaven and the Lord shines upon it with His light, making her live upright, not like the woman bowed down toward the earth (Lk 13:11-16), but standing upright, seeing in God the secret of her strength and her striving. She hears Him say to her: "I am thy shield" (Gen 15:1), and through Him she is protected from all the fiery darts of the enemy (Eph 6:16).

He likened her neck to the tower of David, for David represents the faith that fought Goliath the giant and overcame him, saying to him: "Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts" (1 Sam 17:45). David the prophet declared in his Psalms that God is his refuge and the fortress of his life, and at the same time he does not cease to strive.

It was the custom of the mighty commanders to hang their shields on the tower in remembrance of their brilliant victories and to display their heroism; so the believers use this spiritual tower, which is faith, as the center of their victory in Christ Jesus and their triumph over the evil enemy.

As for the mention of the number of the shields, "a thousand," it refers to the nature of these weapons, for the number 1000 signifies the heavenly life, as though He says that the weapons of the Church are heavenly and spiritual, as the Apostle Paul says: "For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds" (2 Cor 10:4).

entries.section: Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, I will get me to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense" [5-6].

paragraphs.text: If the Lord Christ appears to the Church girt about the paps with a golden girdle (Rev 1:12), as He presents the Old and New Testaments as two breasts which the Church suckles and is nourished by, then the Church also, being the Church of Christ, has these two Testaments as two breasts by which her children are nourished.

The word of God contained in the two Testaments appears as twin young roes born of one mother, a reference to the completeness of the two Testaments together without distinction between them, for the Old Testament prophesied of the New Testament, and the latter unveiled the former and made it clear.

And we saw that the lily signifies the company of the believers who have become like the Lord Christ Himself, "the lily of the valleys" (Song 2:1), and it signifies the inner energies of man, his emotions and motives, which become food for the word of the living God!

In the face of this praise given to the bride for her inner insight, her modesty, her striving in unity of spirit, her work of preaching, her fruitfulness, her gentleness, her faith and her holding fast to the word of God... the bride declares to her Bridegroom that the secret of all this is the Cross of the Bridegroom and His resurrection; therefore she pledges before Him to go with Him to the mountain of myrrh, entering with Him into the life of suffering and being buried with Him in the tomb, and likewise to go with Him to the hill of frankincense, living all the days of her sojourn in unceasing prayer until the day of eternity breaks and the shadows of time flee away.

entries.section: Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, I will get me to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense" [5-6].

paragraphs.text: And the Bridegroom's expected answer will be:

entries.section: "Thou art all fair, my love; there is no blemish in thee" [7].

paragraphs.text: It is as though He concludes His speech by saying: The speech would be long in describing the beauty of her who went out with Me into the fellowship of My sufferings and entered with Me into the life of prayer and fellowship. I perceive in you all beauty, because My love for you hides all your weaknesses, and My blood covers all your sins, bringing out every beauty with which I adorn you, so I see no blemish in you at all.

St. Jerome comments on this speech of the Bridegroom thus: [What is more beautiful than the soul that is called the daughter of God (Ps 45:10), that does not seek for herself outward adornment (1 Pet 3:2)? She believes in Christ, and as His Spirit is given to her, she takes her way toward Christ, who is her Bridegroom and her Lord at the same time, with great hope].

entries.section: A call to work and striving:

paragraphs.text: "Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse, with me from Lebanon: look from the top of Faith (Amana), from the top of Shenir and Hermon, from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards" [8].

If at the beginning of the meeting with the Bridegroom the soul feels much consolation and rest, yet let her know that she is called to set out with her Bridegroom, in His company, to a life of lawful spiritual striving. It is noticed in this call, which the Lord repeats, the following:

It is a call to go out with the Bridegroom, for the spiritual war is the Lord's, on His account and in His name; if the soul goes out sheltering in Him she conquers and triumphs, without Him she knows only defeat.

If the call here is directed to the soul to go out with her spiritual Bridegroom from Libanus, as it came in the Septuagint, she is thereby called to set out through the life of prayer (because Libanus is derived from frankincense) to enter into confrontation with the lions and leopards, for the Christian life is not merely consolations in the chamber but also a fierce war against the evil powers of the spirit, against the devil and sin. Truly Peter longed to remain with the Lord on the mount of Transfiguration, saying to Him: "Lord, it is good for us to be here," but the Lord compelled him to come down with his two companions to face the events of the Cross.

And if the call is directed to going out with Him from Lebanon, which is a tourist country known for a life of luxury, then the heavenly Bridegroom calls the human soul to accompany Him, to go out of the easy life, the life of bodily comfort, and to face the struggle with the powers of darkness, while in the company of her Bridegroom, the conqueror of the lions and leopards.

As for the marks of going out, they are that she sets out from the top of faith (Amana), and through faith she is able to enter to the top of Hermon, to a life of deprivation and voluntary renunciation, practicing the Cross within her, by emptying herself through faith of the lusts and desires of the flesh, to live in a state of satisfaction in Christ Jesus alone. She says by faith with the Apostle Paul: "And having food and raiment let us be therewith content" (1 Tim 6:8), "I have learned both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me" (Phil 4:12-13). And through this inner life, alive in Christ Jesus, the soul enters into the war to overcome by Christ Jesus the lions and leopards.

This is the starting point of the life of victory, which is a crossing with the victorious Lord from the beginning of faith to enter into a fierce war, indeed into spiritual victory and a crossing over to eternity.

St. Augustine commented on this call, declaring that the call here is not a crossing with Christ but a crossing to Him, that is, an entrance into union with Him to practice the spiritual married life, saying: [Cross over to me from the top of faith... for faith is the beginning of marriage].

St. Augustine also sees that it is a crossing of the bride to the heavenly Father through her union with the Bridegroom Christ, for he says: [She comes as the chariot of God, containing thousands of rejoicing men, going forward successfully and crossing this world to the Father, as her Bridegroom Himself, who crossed this world to the Father, brings her across: "I will that these be with me where I am," and by this they pass through the beginning of faith].

St. Gregory of Nyssa sees in these phrases a declaration of the increasing, limitless thirst of the bride to follow her Bridegroom, for he says: [Whoever arises directing himself toward God experiences continually a constant inclination toward increasing progress]. And he interprets the Bridegroom's phrase "Come with me from Lebanon Libanus, my spouse" thus:

[By this He meant: You have done well in that you have arisen with Me until now, and you have come with Me to the mountain of incense. You were buried with Me in Baptism unto death, but you arose and ascended in the fellowship of My divinity... And now rise up from here and come to two other summits, so that you grow and ascend continually through knowledge... Since you have attained this height, do not stop continuing to climb... This frankincense is the beginning of your faith by which you shared in the resurrection. It is the beginning of your advance to receive greater graces. Cross over and come from this beginning, that is, faith, and you will reach, but you will not cease from crossing over continually and continuing to arise].

The saint sees in her being called to cross over with Him "from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards" that man, whom sin had made a ravening beast like the lion and the leopard, has turned away from this nature... But the Bridegroom fears for His bride lest she relapse into sin again, therefore He calls her to go out always from the works of her old man; it is a call to continual striving joined with the life of faith...

entries.section: A call to work and striving:

paragraphs.text: At any rate, as her Bridegroom calls her to cross over with Him through the life of faith with continual striving and struggle against the spiritual beasts, she feels at times the bitterness of this struggle, so she lifts her inner eyes to Him seeking His help, and she hears Him answer her thus:
"Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck" [9].

At the beginning of her relationship with God He brought her into Lebanon, as the bridegroom does with his bride, for he often begins the married life with her in a tourist area far from the cares of life, where they get to know one another. But the married life will not remain so always; rather they must leave Lebanon to live in the marital home, striving and toiling... and so the Lord called her to go out with Him from Lebanon to face the lions and leopards in their dens. Or to go out with Him from mount Lebanon to a life of struggle against the works of the old man, which are like ferocious beasts.
In the midst of her bitter striving she groans within herself and her heart weeps, but He cannot bear her groaning and tears... so His heart is drawn to her, and her inward sighing captivates Him.

St. Gregory of Nyssa noticed that the Bridegroom here says "with one of thine eyes," because man has two kinds of sight, the outward sight by which he sees visible things, and the inward sight by which he beholds God... which is the heart. Here what captivates the heart of God is the tears of the secret inward sight.

As a heavenly Bridegroom He understands the heart of His bride; He cares for her at the time of her striving and her sufferings, and does not require words from her, but understands the language of her inner eyes... When Peter the Apostle fell into denying his Lord there were no words with which he could apologize, but the Lord knew what was in his heart through his tears. And when the sinful woman entered the house of Simon the Pharisee there was no room for speech, but the Lord, the searcher of hearts, said: "Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much" (Lk 7:47).
And the Church has taught us to speak with the Lord in this language, the language of tears, at the close of every day, saying:

entries.section: "Unto thee lift I up mine eyes, O thou that dwellest in the heavens,

paragraphs.text: behold, they are as the eyes of servants unto the hand of their masters, and as the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress.
So our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until that he have mercy upon us.

Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mercy upon us: for we are many times filled with contempt, and our souls are many times filled with shame, which I repeat against them that are at ease, and the contempt against the proud. Alleluia" (Ps 122).

And the Lord's answer will be: I cannot bear your brokenness and your contempt. You have captivated My heart and all My love, so I do not call you servants but beloved ones. You are My brethren. You are My bride!

In a letter which St. Jerome sent to a blind priest in Baetica in Spain he spoke of the eye that captivates the heart of God, saying to him: [It is fitting for you not to grieve because of your deprivation of the two bodily eyes, in which ants and flies and creeping things share with all men, but rather to rejoice that you have the eye of which it was said in the Song of Songs: "Thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes." This eye beholds God, and Moses referred to it when he said: "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight" (Ex 3:3). And we hear of philosophers of this world who put out their eyes so that their thoughts might turn entirely to the depths of their pure mind...].

God's heart is captivated by the language of the eyes broken before Him, as it is also captivated by the language of self-giving and obedience; for He says: "Thou hast ravished my heart... with one chain of thy neck." What is this chain that adorns the inner neck of the soul but the bearing of the yoke and obedience to the divine commandment? For it is written in the Book of Proverbs: "My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother: for they are a crown of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck" (Prov 1:8-9). So the bride is adorned by her accepting the instructions of her Father (God) with joy and gladness and her keeping the law of her mother (the Church)! In other words, she bears upon her neck the yoke of obedience, which is the easy yoke of Christ.

entries.section: Now what have the sufferings of striving done to us?

paragraphs.text: If in the midst of sufferings we feel our weakness and lift our inner eyes in humility toward our God who is in our depths, we draw His heart and captivate His love by our contrition, and He declares the truth of our position, that we are in a position of strength, not weakness, and of glory, not contempt. If we groan through our sense of weakness, He yet confirms to us the truth hidden from our eyes: that our striving, despite all that appears in it of weakness, declares the sweetness of our love, and gives off a fragrance of ointments unique in their spices, for He says:

entries.section: "How pleasant is thy love (thy breasts), my sister, my spouse?!

paragraphs.text: How much better is thy love than wine?!
How much better is the smell of thine ointments than all spices!" [10].
The words of the Bridegroom came matching the words of the bride in her praise of Him, but in a more wonderful and stronger form... How far are these words from the bride's saying:
"For thy (love) breasts are better than wine, because of the savour of thy good ointments..." (Song 1:2-3).

While we say to Him: "For thy breasts are better than wine," He says to us: "How pleasant is thy love (thy breasts), my sister, my spouse?! How much better is thy love than wine!" We commune with Him: "because of the savour of thy good ointments," but He says strongly: "How much better is the smell of thine ointments than all spices?!"

Wonderful is the Lord in His regard for us and in His praise of us, although the love which we carry is only a reflection of His love in us, and the fragrance of spices which we carry is only the fruit of His spices at work in us! How marvelous: He gives us what is His, then returns and ascribes it to us, and praises us for it and rewards us for it.!!

St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, sees the sublimity of the Church of the New Testament through the fragrance that breathes from her, for she is "better than all spices," surpassing the fragrance of every worship offered previously, for he says:

[The mystery of the truth accomplished through the message of the Gospel is alone sweet to God, and is reckoned more sublime than all the spices of the Law, for it is no longer hidden behind a symbol or a shadow, but its fragrance is breathed forth in a clear and open declaration of the truth. If one of the previous spices pleased the Lord as a sweet savour, the secret of its acceptance was not the loftiness of its material or its appearance which were used in the acts of worship, but the meaning which it declared through these acts. This is clear from the great saying of the prophet: "I will take no bullock out of thy house, nor he goats out of thy folds... for I will not eat the flesh of bulls, nor drink the blood of goats" (Ps 49:9, 13)].

But now it is no longer animal sacrifices but the unique Sacrifice which the Father smells as a savour of acceptance... through this Sacrifice God smells all our worship and all our spiritual striving as a sweet fragrance "better than all spices."

entries.section: "How pleasant is thy love (thy breasts), my sister, my spouse?!

paragraphs.text: Therefore in the midst of our bitterness because of our feeling of weakness, the Lord praises us without flattery or hypocrisy, but returns and speaks in more detail about the blessing of fellowship in sufferings with Him, or striving for His sake and in His name, saying:

entries.section: "Thy lips, O my spouse, drop honey,

paragraphs.text: honey and milk are under thy tongue; and the smell of thy garments is like the smell of frankincense" [11].

What does the Lord see in His striving, suffering bride? He sees her as the bee, of which it is said: "The bee is little among such as fly; but her honey is the sweetest of foods" (Sir 3:11). St. Gregory of Nyssa comments on this, saying: [The bee is loved by everyone and esteemed by all, for although her strength is weak she carries a heavenly wisdom and always strives to attain the life of perfection]. This is the secret of the honey which drops from the lips of the bride and the honey under her tongue, therefore the saint says: [It is fitting for us to fly over the meadows of inspired teachings, and to gather from each of them into our storehouses of wisdom. Thus honey is formed within us, as that sweet produce which is stored in our hearts as in a beehive, and through the various teachings storehouses are formed in our memory after the likeness of the waxen cells which do not perish. We must be like the bee, for her honey is sweet and her sting does not harm, busy in the important work of virtue. She is truly occupied in turning the toils of this life into eternal blessings, and offering her labor for the health of kings and herbs. So also the soul attracts the Bridegroom, and the angels admire her, who complete her strength in weakness through honored wisdom].
What else does the Lord see in His striving, suffering bride? He sees her as the holy land that floweth with milk and honey (Ex 3:8, 17).

The Lord presented His striving, suffering bride in the most wonderful picture, for if the Lord promised His people of old a land flowing with milk and honey to be for them a place of bodily rest and a place of bodily satisfaction and a center for worship upon it, then His bride in her turn becomes herself the Lord's place of rest; the Holy Trinity rests within her, and she overflows from the fruit of the Spirit with milk and honey which God and His angels desire and in which the saints rejoice, and it even overflows to unbelievers.
In the midst of the believer's sufferings the Lord sees his lips dropping honey and his tongue hiding honey and his breast filled with spiritual milk.

As for the honey which drops from his lips, it signifies the words of grace that come from the mouth of the believer, few, falling like drops (dropping), but sweet and delightful! They give the hearer a blessing and inward sweetness and rest in the soul!
As for the honey, it is like a hidden treasure "under the tongue" which the believer presents to others without ostentation or love of display... a treasure and food suited to the mature.!

What can this hidden honey be but the "word of God" the living, who was called the heavenly manna, whose type was the manna that came down upon the people of old, "and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey" (Ex 16:31). When Ezekiel the prophet ate the word of God he said: "it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness" (Ezek 3:3), and the psalmist described it thus: "How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" (Ps 119:103), "the judgments of the LORD are true and righteous altogether. More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb" (Ps 19:9-10). Solomon the wise also asked us to enjoy eating the good word of God when he said: "My son, eat thou honey, because it is good" (Prov 24:13), "Pleasant words are as a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones" (Prov 16:24).

At any rate, when the Lord speaks of His care for His people He assures them that He gave them honey as a reference to the sweetness of His gift, or the sweetness of His word in their mouth, for He says: "Thou didst eat fine flour, and honey, and oil: and thou wast exceeding beautiful, and wast fit for the kingdom" (Ezek 16:13), "with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee" (Ps 81:16), "He made him to suck honey out of the rock" (Deut 32:13). The honey of the word of God is the secret of the beauty of His people so that they are fit to become a queen, and the secret of her satisfaction and her being watered: He who feeds His people with honey returns and finds this honey of His hidden under the tongue of His bride, and so He rejoices in her.!

If the Lord presents His honey through the tongue of His bride to satisfy the mature, He fills her breast with unadulterated milk so that the children find for themselves a place in His Church and rest with His bride. And as St. Gregory of Nyssa says: [The man who knows how to speak with every kind of person and has under his tongue different powers of the divine word (honey and milk) is the one who is able to give each one what suits him according to his capacities at the right time].

We all know that man in the midst of his sufferings and afflictions forgoes his clothing, but the Bridegroom here smells the fragrance of the bride in the midst of her sufferings as the fragrance of pure prayer (frankincense)! He listens to her sighs and her petitions because she is in a state of suffering! He gives ear to her and answers her requests because she is broken-hearted! By this the believer, in his spiritual striving, puts off his earthly garments in order that the Holy Spirit may clothe him with the garments of heaven which do not wear out: "love, joy, peace..." (Gal 5:22). This is the work of the Spirit in the life of the suffering bride!

entries.section: "Thy lips, O my spouse, drop honey,

paragraphs.text: Finally, man often looks at himself in the time of affliction and thinks he is in a wasteland without inhabitant, barren without fruit, but the Lord sees the opposite, for He says:

entries.section: "A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse;

paragraphs.text: a spring shut up, a fountain sealed" [12].

It is as though He says to her: Remember the complete potentialities within you, you are a garden and a spring and a fountain, the potentialities of the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, which are not revealed in you unless you accept sufferings and your back is bowed to the Cross.

entries.section: Why was the bride called a garden inclosed and a fountain sealed?

paragraphs.text: 1. St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that the garden contains different kinds of trees. Their fruit is bitter at first, but at the right time, when it ripens, it is sweet and beneficial, delighting all the senses... So the soul in her spiritual life, as the Lord Himself plants her and waters her, bears sufferings and toils and bitterness... and at the right time brings forth fruit that delights souls. 2. The saint speaks of the secret of her being enclosed, saying: [Our garden is enclosed on every side by the wall of the commandments so that no thief or ravening beast may steal into it. It is enclosed by the fence of the commandments so that no wild boar can approach it]. 3. If the garden needs a spring or a fountain, the spring must be shut up and the fountain sealed, and as the wise man says: "Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well. Let not thy fountains be dispersed abroad, nor rivers of waters in the streets. Let them be only thine own, and not strangers' with thee. Let thy fountain be blessed" (Prov 5:15-18). So the divine inspiration commands us not to waste the waters of our fountains outside, in the streets, with strangers... And as St. Gregory says, when our inner thoughts turn aside toward sin (the stranger) we have lost the waters of our fountains and given them to strangers. [It is purity which seals this fountain so that it may be for its Lord].

St. Ambrose sees that the sealed fountain is Baptism, which remains sealed and shut if it is not usurped by deeds and declared by words. By Baptism we have become a paradise in which is the possibility of life and fruit-bearing, but a paradise inclosed, and a spring able to burst forth pure and sweet waters that water many but it is shut up, and a fountain sealed which if opened would burst forth springs of living water.!

We may think of ourselves that we are empty, but God sees within us a paradise and a spring and a fountain that it is not right to open except to Him, for He is the only Bridegroom of the soul, who has the right to enter the garden of the heart and drink the springs of His love! In other words, the soul as a bride is committed to remain in her virginity longing for the heavenly Bridegroom alone, opening to Him her heart and her feelings and her emotions and all her energy, as the chaste virgin awaiting her bridegroom (Mt 25), as a member of the Church of the firstborn.

St. Ambrose has a beautiful comment, for he says: [The Lord utters this saying to the Church whom He wants to be a virgin without defilement and without blemish. The fertile garden is virginity, which can bear much fruit having a good fragrance... It is a garden inclosed because it is surrounded on every side by the wall of purity. And it is a fountain sealed because virginity is the fountain and source of chastity, keeping the seal of purity preserved without decay, in which the image of God is reflected, where the purity of simplicity agrees also with the purity of the body].

St. Ambrose linked this seal with the mystery of the Eucharist, for he saw in Christ's speech here about the Church a commandment from the Bridegroom toward His bride who feeds on His most holy Body and precious Blood, keeping these Mysteries in her life sealed, not loosing them by works of evil and the loss of purity.
St. Augustine sees that this garden inclosed is the Church, for he says:

[Paradise is the Church as she was called in the Song of Songs, and the four rivers of Paradise are the four Gospels, and the fruit-bearing trees are the saints, and the fruits are their works, and the tree of life is the Holy of Holies, that is, Christ, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is freedom of will, for if a man despises the will of God he destroys himself, and then he learns the difference between sanctifying himself for the common good and what he does according to his own will].
And finally, many of the Fathers saw in St. Mary the Virgin "the garden inclosed," and in this she represents the virgin Church which is sanctified to the Lord alone. St. Augustine says:

[Christ Himself is a virgin, and His mother is also a virgin. Yes, although she is His mother she is still a virgin, for Jesus entered into her "the doors being shut" (Jn 20:19), He entered His new tomb hewn out in the solid rock in which no man before or after had lain (Jn 19:41). So Mary is "a garden inclosed... a fountain sealed." From this fountain flows, as Joel says (Joel 2:18), the river that waters the torrent from the briers and thorns, the briers of the sins which we committed and by which we were bound (Prov 5:22), and the thorns which choke the seed that the owner of the land sowed (Mt 13:7)...].

entries.section: Why was the bride called a garden inclosed and a fountain sealed?

paragraphs.text: Therefore the garden inclosed or the spring shut up or the fountain sealed signifies the life which none enters but the Lord alone, who has the key of David, "he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth" (Rev 3:7). This life bears the precious heavenly fruits of the Holy Spirit, for He says:

entries.section: "Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits; camphire, with spikenard,

paragraphs.text: spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense;
myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices:
a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon (frankincense)" [13-15].

What does the Lord find in us? He finds various kinds of fruits to eat such as the pomegranate, and sweet fragrances and spices and incense (frankincense) and materials used as good ointments and living waters to drink...

Thus the bride of Christ appears rich in everything: she has food that satisfies, and drink that quenches, and precious spices for adornment, and medicines for healing... Her Bridegroom and His friends rejoice in her. It is noticed in the mentioned phrases that the word "all" is repeated, so she lacks nothing, but is sufficient in everything. This is the expression which the Apostle Paul used in describing the believers, for he says: "God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work" (2 Cor 9:8). "We also, since the day we heard it, do not cease to pray for you, and to desire that ye might be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding; that ye might walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing, being fruitful in every good work, and increasing in the knowledge of God; strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness" (Col 1:9-11).

The following are examples of the many plants which the soul carried within her, although I have already spoken of some of them in some detail. 1. An orchard of pomegranates: We saw the cheek of the bride like a piece of a pomegranate filled with redness, a sign of spiritual beauty through the blood of the Lord Christ, as well as a sign of modesty in gentleness and calm... She carries the beauty of the love of God and His gentleness...

St. Gregory of Nyssa speaks of the pomegranate tree, saying: [The pomegranate tree makes the thief despair of it, for its branches are fenced with thorns, and its fruit is covered with an exceedingly bitter and rough rind which protects it. But when the fruit ripens at the right time, as its rind is removed and you look inside it you find sweet fruit, attractive in appearance, delicious in taste like honey, with the flavor of wine... So it is fitting for us also not to be pampered in striving nor lovers of luxury in this life, but to choose the way of the chaste (self-controlled) hard life. By this thieves cannot approach the fruit of virtue, because it is fortified by the rough covering of self-control, and surrounded by a hard and stern way of life, as though it were thorns that prick whoever approaches it with an evil purpose. But at the right time we enjoy what the pomegranate offers of a mixture of delight in diverse kinds of fruit...]. 2. Camphire (henna): It was spoken of before; the bride uses it for adornment on the night before her wedding to prepare herself for the bridegroom with a sweet fragrance, and she dyes her hands and feet with it to make them red. 3. Spikenard: It is extracted from a small plant that grows abundantly on the Himalayan mountains, at a height of about 1100-1700 feet above sea level. It is a very costly ointment used in trade. With it Mary the sister of Lazarus anointed the feet of the Lord (Jn 12:13), and she or another poured it on His head six days before the Passover (Mk 14:3) as a sign of her love and thanks to Him. 4. Saffron: its flower is somewhat violet in color, with red veins, but the saffron itself is yellow in color, ground and mixed with olive oil to be used as an ointment. Saffron is used in food as a kind of spice, and it is also used in medicines. 5. Calamus: a wood with a sweet fragrance, from which an oil is extracted that is used in matters pertaining to the sacrifice (Isa 43:24; Jer 6:20). 6. Cinnamon: a kind of wood with a sweet fragrance, which some Easterners use instead of tea; it was used as one of the compounds of the holy oil for sanctifying Aaron and his sons (Ex 20:22), and it is still used as one of the ingredients of the oil of the Myron when it is cooked, and it was also used as a kind of medicine. 7. Finally the Bridegroom communes with her, saying: "A fountain of gardens, living waters, and streams from frankincense," for she carries within her her Bridegroom, the living Fountain who waters His plants and His vines inside His inclosed garden, who takes hold of her with streams that sweep away all that she has toward eternity...

entries.section: The bride shares with her Bridegroom

paragraphs.text: "Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind, blow upon my garden, that its spices may flow out.
Let my beloved come down to His garden, and eat His precious fruit" [16].

At the wedding feast the Bridegroom praised His bride and called her to go out with Him outside the camp, to share His sufferings and His crucifixion, and to be anointed with myrrh and so be buried with Him, that she might rise with Him bearing many and varied plants, which are the work of His resurrection in her. Now the bride addresses Him and asks that the north wind, full of cold, and the hot south wind blow upon her garden... so that her spices may flow out, and her Bridegroom may come down to her and enjoy His fruits in her... What, then, does the bride mean by the north wind and the south wind? 1. In Greek the word "wind" is the same as the word "spirit"... Perhaps the bride here is asking her Bridegroom to send her His Holy Spirit, who pursues her from every side, so that He may give her the abundant fruit in which the Bridegroom rejoices. 2. The call to the wind to blow upon her is a call to the Beloved Himself, as the gentle and meek wind who passes through the heart and dwells in it, so that "the work of Christ" may be done in us. 3. Perhaps the soul meant by the wind some outward circumstances, for since she has become a closed garden consecrated to the Lord, she is not afraid of what surrounds her, for "all things work together for good to them that love God" (Rom 8:28). If the Apostle Paul was given honor, it turned out to the furtherance of the Gospel, and if he was bound in the inner prison, his bonds turned out all the more to the furtherance of the Gospel (Phil 1:12), or as he says of himself, "Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death" (Phil 1:20). 4. The wind also signifies trials, for if northern trials blow upon the soul, that is, if sin is stirred up against her, or right-hand trials, as when self-righteousness rises up within her... in all this the Lord upholds her, not only to keep her from trials but to bring forth from them fruits in which the Bridegroom rejoices! He is like Samson, who brought forth food out of the eater, and found sweetness in the strong!

It is to be noted that the soul calls her heart "my garden," that is, her own, but she quickly calls her Bridegroom, saying, "Let my beloved come down to His garden." For she is His vineyard, the work of His hands and under His care; He is in the midst of her, so she shall not be moved. The soul cannot let her spices flow in the midst of trials unless she surrenders herself to Him to be His garden, that He may care for her and eat of her fruit, which is "His fruit."

She calls Him to come down to her, for the heart is His, and the fruit is ascribed to Him... St. Ambrose saw that the call is directed to the Bridegroom to come down to the soul in the font of Baptism, to receive His garden and work in it by His Holy Spirit so that she may bring forth His fruit, as he says:

["Let my beloved come down to His garden, and eat the fruit of the apple tree that is His." Truly, what a beautiful tree, full of fruit, whose roots stretch out in the waters (of Baptism) of the holy spring!]. He came down to her by His Incarnation, by His crucifixion and His entering the tomb, and He comes down to her at her baptism in the holy spring, and she still asks Him to come down to her, coming upon the clouds, to take her with Him, for she has borne His fruits within her!

entries.section: The beginning of married life

paragraphs.text: No sooner had the Church called her Bridegroom to come down to her to eat from His garden within her, full of the plants of His Holy Spirit and watered from the holy spring of Baptism, than He answered her call at once without hesitation, saying:

"I have come down into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten my honeycomb (my bread) with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk; eat, O friends; drink, and be drunk, O beloved" [1].

He hastened to come down to His garden without hesitation, because the call here accorded with His will, and so found a swift response in the eyes of God. She called Him to come down to His garden, to which He desires to come down at all times. For if the Lord from eternity prepared the events of salvation so that they became the object of His delight and pleasure, in spite of the shame, suffering, and death they carried, as the Apostle Paul says: "for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame" (Heb 12:3), then His bride calls Him to come down to the very garden He entered on the night of His passion, and to that in which His body was laid in the tomb. She calls Him to see her as she fills up what is lacking of the afflictions in her body (Col 1:24), that is, shares His sufferings and His crucifixion and His burial; therefore the Lord does not hesitate to say: "I have gathered my myrrh with my spices"... as though the events of salvation had become alive and extended in the life of His children!

Father Rufinus sees that the garden here is none other than the place where the Lord was crucified, where the wise man declares that the Bridegroom drinks wine mingled with myrrh, which was offered to the Lord at the moment of His crucifixion.

The Lord accepted the call at once, for He found that everything that belongs to the bride is His own: her title is His garden, and she is His sister and His bride, and within her He found His myrrh and His spices, His honeycomb and His honey, His wine and His milk. He found the fruits of His Holy Spirit within her and hastened to her, and He found within her no hire of iniquity or hire of a harlot or any other of the things that He does not accept, as He says: "Thou shalt not bring the hire of a whore, or the price of a dog, into the house of the LORD thy God for any vow: for even both these are abomination unto the LORD thy God" (Deut 23:18).
Before explaining what is inside the garden, St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, asked:
"Who is this whom she invites to the banquet that she has prepared?"

He is the One from whom and by whom all things exist (1 Cor 1:17), who gives help to everyone in due season (Lk 12:43), who opens His hand and satisfies every living thing with blessing (Ps 145:16), who comes down as the heavenly Bread (Jn 6:14), giving life to the world, and pours out from Himself alone life upon all creation.

This is the One for whom the bride prepared her table, and the table is a garden planted with living trees. The trees are we ourselves, and the fruit that we offer is our souls, as He said when He took on the fullness of our humanity: "My meat is to do the will of my Father" (Jn 4:34). The aim of His divine will is plain, for He wills that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim 2:4).
Therefore the food that is prepared is our salvation, and the fruit is our free will, which offers to God "our souls," as though they were fruit gathered from the branch.

It is fitting for us also to contemplate the bride, who formerly enjoyed the fruit of the apple tree, saying: "his fruit was sweet to my taste" (Song 2:3); but now she herself has become sweet, a ripe fruit offered to the vinedresser, who enjoys it.

As for the expression "Let my beloved come down" [1], it is in its wording a petition like the prayers "Hallowed be thy name" and "Thy will be done." Just as the form of these two phrases carries a prayer, so the bride prays, saying: "Let (my friend) come down," declaring to God the abundance of the fruit of her perfection.
His coming down requires the work of His divine love, for we cannot ascend to the Most High unless the Lord stands by the lowly and lifts up the meek (Ps 147:6) [Ps 146 LXX].
So that the soul may rise to heaven, she seeks the help of God on high, beseeching Him to come down from His majesty and be united with us here who are below.

The answer came through the prophet thus: "Then shalt thou call... and he shall say, Here I am" (Isa 58:9); indeed, even before the bride lifts up her prayer He hears her petition and gives ear to the preparation of her heart [(Ps 10:17) Septuagint].

He comes to His garden... and gathers its spices, full of the fruit of her virtues; then He speaks of His enjoyment of the banquet and His delight in it, saying to His bride: "I have come down into my garden, my sister, my bride...".

St. Gregory of Nyssa He comes down into the heart and dwells in it and rests; He gathers its myrrh with its spices... that is, He gathers the fruits of the Cross (the myrrh) with the blessings of His holy tomb (the spices). He sees that the cup of our myrrh is His own cup, and the spices with which we are shrouded are the spices of His burial... He sees us bearing His cross and buried with Him to the world.

Within us He eats His honeycomb and His honey, as though He had entered the Promised Land that flows with milk and honey. He eats the same two kinds of food, "the honeycomb and the honey," of which He ate with His disciples after His resurrection, proving in many ways that He is alive, risen from the dead, remaining at work in the midst of His Church.
He finds everything in our heart sweet and delectable, like the honeycomb and the honey.
He drinks also His wine, that is, His love which He poured into us by His Holy Spirit, with His unadulterated milk, that is, purity and chastity...

Then He invites His friends and His beloved to enter with Him into His own garden, that they may be satisfied and rejoice over His bride. Who are these friends and beloved? They are the heavenly ones who rejoice over one sinner who repents more than over ninety and nine just persons who need no repentance (Lk 15:7). These enter the heart with the Lord not to reign but as soldiers of the heavenly King, friends of the Bridegroom, saying with St. John the Baptist: "He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom's voice" (Jn 3:29).
The following are excerpts from the sayings of the Fathers about these friends and their work in the heart:
* The heart is the palace of Christ; into it the King enters to rest, and with Him the angels and the spirits of the saints; there He dwells and walks, and within it He establishes His kingdom!

St. Macarius the Great * He does not stand alone, but the angels go before Him, saying: "Lift up your gates, O ye princes." Which gates are these? Those of which the psalmist sings in another place, saying: "Open to me the gates of righteousness" (Ps 19:1).
Therefore open your gates to Christ, that He may enter into you; open the gates of purity, the gates of courage, the gates of wisdom.
Believe the message of the angels: Lift up your everlasting gates, that the King of glory may come in, the Lord of Sabaoth (of hosts).
St. Ambrose Therefore let us open the heart to God and His angels, that there may be heavenly joy within us.

entries.section: Shadows in married life

paragraphs.text: "I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved (my near one) that knocketh, saying,
Open, open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one: for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.
I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on?
I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?" [2-3].

What an accurate picture of the mutual dealings between God and man! For a long time man lived relaxed and neglectful of his salvation, in spite of all the means God gave him to be watchful. God wanted to make him a son of light and of the day, but man insisted on turning all the time of his exile into night, which he spends asleep, even though his heart is awake.

God gave humanity the natural law to awaken their hearts, so that they are without excuse; but "when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened. Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, and changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things" (Rom 1:21-23).

And He gave them the written Law, but since they sinned in the Law, they fell under judgment by the Law, "for not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified" (Rom 2:13); so the holy Law, or the commandment which is holy, and just, and good, revealed sin to me and exposed it, so sin revived and I died (Rom 7).

And God sent His prophets, but what did humanity do to them? The Lord Himself says: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!" (Mt 23:37).

And finally, "the voice of my beloved that knocketh"... The Word of God Himself came down to man to knock at the door of his heart... He stands before the soul begging her to open to Him. The Sun of Righteousness came down and entered our time, which we had made night, to shine upon us who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, that we might arise from our heedlessness!

Perhaps the discourse here concerns the soul that called the Messiah her Bridegroom, but then relaxed in her love for Him. Sleep overcame her and she could not watch with Him on the night of His passion, though her heart, the dwelling of the Holy Spirit, in which there is life, rebukes her! She grew lukewarm in her love for Him, but God, the Lover of mankind, sees her heart awake and does not cease to come down to her door and call her: "Open, open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my perfect one..."

The voice of the Beloved here reproaches gently, so that it does not wound the feelings of the heart, but encourages His bride, calling her His sister, His friend, His dove, His perfect one... though she is sound asleep! He does not rebuke her nor reprove her, but gives her hope and encourages her.

As for His repeating the request: "Open, open to me..." it may perhaps show the repeated call to humanity in the two Testaments, the Old and the New, for God has not changed, nor has His call changed, since He asks that the heart open to Him and receive Him!

In the repetition of the call there is also a declaration of the perfect freedom of the soul, for He is the Creator and Lord and King, yet He does not force His way into the soul, but entreats her to open to Him... In the book of Revelation we see Him say: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me" (Rev 3:20); even when He came to His disciples walking on the sea in the midst of the great tempest, He did not force His way into their boat, but the Evangelist says: "Then they willingly received him into the ship" (Jn 6:20).

St. Athanasius the Apostolic used this friendly speech of the Lord Christ to the human soul in his book "History of the Arians" as an argument against their use of violence, saying: [When He (the Lord) comes to anyone He does not need to open by force, but He knocks at the door, saying: "Open to me, my sister, my bride"; if it is opened to Him, He enters, and if it delays, He departs and does not enter. He uses persuasion and counsel when He preaches the truth, and does not use swords and soldiers. But what persuasion is this, when the terror of the emperor prevails?!].

He persuades her to open to Him by love, for she has become His sister and He her firstborn brother, who is able to help her. He became "the firstborn among many brethren" (Rom 8:39); He broke through the door of death and shattered it, becoming the firstfruits of them that slept (1 Cor 15:20)... Let her open her heart to Him who opened for her the door of life!

He returns and begs her to open by the strong friendship between them, for He calls her "His friend," which is the title by which Abraham, the father of believers, was called (2 Chr 20:7; Isa 41:8; Jas 2:23). If God opened the secrets of His heart to His friend Abraham, saying: "Shall I hide from Abraham that thing which I do?" (Gen 18:17)... how much more fitting it is for the believer, who has become a friend of God, to open his heart fully to Him.
He draws her to open the doors of her heart by calling her "His dove," since she bore within her the "Holy Spirit," who came down in the form of a dove, and so she has the power to open her heart.
And finally He encourages her to do so, since she is "the perfect one" who is without blemish, so she cannot close the door in His face.

Thus God deals with us: He instructs us not through commands and prohibitions but by declaring His love and friendship, and makes clear to us our standing in relation to Him, and reveals to us the potentialities of His Holy Spirit working in us, and encourages us by what we have attained!
Finally He entreats her as the "bearer of sorrows and griefs" for her sake, saying to her:
"For my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night" [2].

If you have made your time a night without day, so that your life has become sleep, then in love I break into time and enter this night, not to sleep but to bear the terrors of the night for you. Indeed the Lord entered the garden at night while His disciples slept and could not watch with Him one hour (Mt 26:40), but He went into the depths to receive the cup of suffering that He might drink it for all humanity... In the garden He "began to be sorrowful and very heavy" (Mt 26:37). He cried: "My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death," and the drops of sweat poured down like blood!!!

He speaks to her and asks her to open to Him for the sake of what He endured on her account that stormy, rainy night, for His head was filled with dew and His locks with the drops of the night... He bore the divine wrath in His body, and as the prophet says: "Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed" (Isa 53:4-5).
But she offered unfitting human excuses and spoke without concern; she did not call Him her Lord or her master, nor even call Him by His name, nor mention any of His titles, but said:
"I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on?!

entries.section: Shadows in married life

paragraphs.text: I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?" [3].

What feeble arguments the soul presents in her spiritual lukewarmness... an excuse for not opening the heart to the One of whom she knows fully that He loves her. It is a picture of man, who begrudged himself bearing a little weariness to achieve the meeting with the Lord Christ, in spite of the great deal that the Lord paid!

How easy it would be for her to wrap a garment around her body and put sandals on her feet... but she was preoccupied with the comfort of her body rather than the enjoyment of her Bridegroom... she resembled those who made excuses so as not to attend the wedding (Mt 22:5).
If she has put off her coat, the Lord Christ Himself is the eternal garment that covers us, as the Apostle Paul says: "ye have put on Christ" (Gal 3:27).

This is the best robe which the heavenly Father brings to the son who returns to Him (Lk 15:22). This is the embroidered garment offered by the hand of God, as the prophet Zechariah says: "I have taken away thine iniquity from thee, and clothed thee with embroidered garments" (Zech 3:4).

If she has put off her garment, He gives her His Spirit to put on, as the secret of life within her, for He assures His disciples: "Behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you: but tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high" (Lk 24:49).

If she has washed her feet, let her know that the One knocking at the door is her Lord, who girds Himself and washes the feet of His bride (Jn 13:5). She washed them with the water of her own righteousness so that her conscience might rest for a while, but when the hands of the Lord reach out to wash her feet she will have rest in His eternal kingdom. Therefore the Lord said to the Apostle Peter: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me" (Jn 13:8). Therefore let us rise from the bed of the "ego," or the "human self," and go to our Bridegroom, who covers us with His blood and clothes us with His Holy Spirit, and also washes our inner life so that we may live as holy to Him.

entries.section: Married love returns through the Cross

paragraphs.text: If the soul cannot listen to the voice of the One who loved her, who declared His love in various ways, there remains for Him to stretch out His wounded hand on the Cross into her mind, that she may see the marks of the wounds of love which He bore for her sake, and her bowels groan for Him, as she says:

"My beloved put forth His hand through the window, and my bowels groaned for Him; I arose to open to my beloved, and my hands dropped with myrrh, and my fingers with flowing myrrh upon the handle of the lock" [4-5].

When the world grew narrow before the disciples because of fear, they shut the doors and set up barricades, not knowing that closed doors would not prevent the Lord, wounded for their sake, from entering to them to show them His hands and His side so that they rejoiced (Jn 20:20). He opened an inner window in their hearts so that they might touch the wounds of His love. Thus the Lord puts forth His wounded hand through the window so that His believers may discover the secret of His love and their bowels groan for Him. I say that this window is none other than the side of the Lord and His wounds, through which the Lord puts forth the hand of His love so that we uncover His inner bowels aflame with love, and our bowels also groan... He loved us first, therefore we also love Him.

The window has special memories in the Old Testament, some of which carried symbolic aspects of God's saving work in the life of His bride; we mention by way of example: 1. Through the window Abimelech perceived that Rebekah was Isaac's wife and not merely his sister (Gen 26:8), and likewise through the wounds of the Lord the Church is declared the bride of Christ Jesus. 2. Through the window the two spies were let down from Rahab's house, which was on the town wall (Josh 2:15), and through it David descended from the house, fleeing from Saul's messengers, and escaped (1 Sam 19:21). Through the window we descend from the pride of this world to cross its walls and escape all the counsels of the devil. 3. The window on which she bound a cord of scarlet threads (Josh 2:12), and through which Rahab the harlot and all her household were saved, is a reference to the wounds of the Lord Christ, which rescued the corrupt company of the Gentiles and all their children who entered the Church, kept in the precious blood of the Lord. 4. As the window was a sign of salvation, it also bore a sign of the destruction of evil, for when Jezebel the wicked queen painted her eyes and adorned her head with the adornment of the world, she was thrown down from the window and the dogs licked her blood (2 Kgs 9). And Ahaziah the wicked king too, who trusted in Baalzebub the god of Ekron and not in the living God, fell down through the lattice in his upper chamber that was in Samaria (2 Kgs 1:2), and was sick and died.
