And in the song of Deborah the judge, she asked the mother of King Sisera to look out of the window (Judg 5:28) to see why the chariots of her son were so long in coming and why the steps of his chariots tarried... for he and his chariots perished. 5. Through this window the bowels of believers groan for the saving love of God, while unbelievers mock these wounds, imitating Michal the daughter of the wicked king Saul, for when she looked through a window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord she despised him in her heart (2 Sam 6:16; 1 Chr 15:29).

We return to the bride, who enjoyed the hand of the Lord that came into her midst and so perceived the secret of His Cross; the hardness of her stony heart was broken, and she arose to open to her beloved. She cried out with the younger son: "I will arise and go to my father" (Lk 15). She declared her longing for the One who loved her by returning to Him through sincere repentance, bitter tears, and pure sighs; therefore she said: "my hands dropped with myrrh, and my fingers with flowing myrrh upon the handle of the lock."

entries.section: Married love returns through the Cross

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that the myrrh signifies "the death which Christ died for us," for we have touched it through repentance and accepted to die with Him, so that the everlasting doors may be opened before us.
"I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had turned and passed on.
My soul went out when He turned away (spoke).
I sought Him, but I did not find Him; I called Him, but He gave me no answer.
The watchmen that go about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me.
The keepers of the walls took away my veil from me.
I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem (by the powers of the field and its virtues), if ye find my beloved, that ye tell Him that I am wounded with love.
What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women!!
What is thy beloved more than another beloved, that thou dost so charge us!" [6-9].

She arose to open to her Bridegroom after a long sleep, but her Bridegroom had left her and passed on. Why did He do so? He disciplines man for his delay in responding, and in His discipline He appears as though He had left us for a time... This leaving in itself is considered a sign of God's concern for us, and Father Daniel gave two reasons for this leaving: 1. God leaves us for a short time that we may be alerted to the weakness of our hearts; then we realize that whatever purity of heart we had before was a free gift through divine visitation. 2. When He leaves us, our heart's aim and our zeal in prayer in seeking the Holy Spirit are revealed within us, that is, it serves as a test for us in perseverance, steadfastness of mind, and true zeal. So when we obtain spiritual happiness and the joy of purity, we hold on to these things with more care, because men in general do not care to keep what they think they can obtain easily.

Father Daniel says: [The blessed prophet David makes known to us that this temporary forsaking on God's part is sometimes for our good, and therefore he asked in his prayer that this forsaking not be perpetual, beseeching Him that it be within certain limits, saying: "O forsake me not utterly" (Ps 119:8). In other words he says: I know that You forsake Your saints for their benefit and in order to test them... Therefore I do not ask that You not forsake me, for it is not profitable for me not to feel my weakness (therefore he said: "and it seems to me that I have been humbled" (Ps 119:71)), nor is it of benefit to me not to have an opportunity for battle. For this opportunity will surely not be given me as long as I am filled with God's constant protection. For Satan does not dare to fight me as long as I rely upon Your protection... So I ask You to leave me, but not utterly (the Greek expression "not exceedingly"), for it is useful for me that You leave me a little so that the steadfastness of my love may be tested...].

Father Daniel spoke much about what we call spiritual lukewarmness because of God's leaving us for a time so that we may be tested, fight, and be proved... but in truth it is not forsaking but divine care, and St. John Chrysostom likened God's attitude to a nurse who holds a child's hands, walks with him a little, then suddenly lifts her hands from him so that he may dare to walk... She takes away her hands but continues to look at him with her heart and mind as her eyes watch him, and her hands are ready to support him.

The human soul says: "I sought Him, but I did not find Him," though He stands beside her, indeed He is within her, waiting to see her striving for His sake, so that she may say with Jacob: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me."
"I called Him, but He gave me no answer," though He is occupied with arranging all things for my salvation.

The soul went about the whole world seeking the One she loves though He was within her, and as St. Augustine said: [In his folly he went out to search for Him outside, in nature and in books, though God was within him, deeper than his depth and higher than his height].

Now who are the watchmen that go about the city who smote her and wounded her, and the keepers of the walls who took away her veil from her? 1. Since the speaker here is the believer in the Church of the New Testament, he reproaches in the name of the Church the company of the Jews and their leaders, who represent the watchmen going about the city of Jerusalem and those responsible for guarding the word of God, since it was fitting for them to be servants of the Word and preachers of the Messiah the Savior, but they seize the Church and smite her and wound her, and have come to defame her...

Before these insults the believer does not turn his gaze away from his Bridegroom, but on the contrary assures those who trouble him that he is wounded by the love of this heavenly Bridegroom, saying: "I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem... if ye find my beloved, that ye tell Him that I am wounded with love."
This is the fifth time that the Church of the Gentiles speaks with the company of the Jews in reproach thus:

a. In the first instance (Song 1:5), she reproaches them because they insulted her, saying of her that she is black like the tents of Kedar, has no origin, did not receive the Law, and no prophets came from her... She answers them that though she is black by virtue of her pagan origin, yet now she is in the bosom of the Father, who joined her to Himself and made her comely through His Son Jesus Christ, who made her comely and made her like the curtains of Solomon.

b. In the second instance (Song 2:7), when she began her union with the Lord, whose left hand is under her head and whose right hand embraces her, the Jews tried to corrupt and destroy this union; but she declared that the day comes in which the Lord will appear and declare the truth of this union.

c. And in the third instance (Song 3:5), when the Bridegroom entered the tomb the Jews stood in the position of those who gloat, as though saying: "Come out of the tomb and we will believe you"; but the Church answers them: Do not suppose that He died and His message passed away, but He is alive, risen from the dead, raising me up with Him and bringing me up from the wilderness white as pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense... through Him she rose to the Father!

d. And in the fourth instance (Song 3:11), when the discourse was about the Cross, the Church asked the Jews to understand that when they crowned Him with thorns in mockery, He was in fact being crowned as the Bridegroom of all humanity on the day of His wedding and the day of the gladness of His heart.

e. This is the fifth time (Song 5:8), where the Church declares to the company of the Jews that though her children passed through some lukewarmness, and it became as though God had forsaken them, yet the Church is still alive, full of love... She strives until the Lord removes their lukewarmness from them. 2. Perhaps the watchmen going about the city refer to the servants of the Church, the city of God, and the keepers of the walls are the preachers of the word; all of these are bound to hide behind the word of God in their speaking with lukewarm souls. These souls feel as though they were smitten by them and wounded, and put to shame and disgrace by the taking away of their veil, because the word of God is like a sword that cuts off evil and drives it away from the soul. It is also like a mirror that exposes man's weaknesses and unveils his depths! So the blows and wounds and nakedness here are not meant to trouble the soul and defame her, but are the wounds of love that lead to sincere repentance. As the Apostle Paul himself says: "For if I make you sorry, who is he then that maketh me glad, but the same which is made sorry by me?" (2 Cor 2:2).

In any case, when lukewarmness is removed from the human soul, she not only realizes her return to the Father's embrace in Christ Jesus, but she bears witness to the power of this work even before unbelievers, who ask, saying:
"What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women!

entries.section: Married love returns through the Cross

paragraphs.text: What is thy beloved more than another beloved, that thou dost so charge us?!" [9].
You are beautiful and lack nothing, so who is this Beloved with whom you are occupied? Who is this unique Beloved by whom you thus charge us for the sake of your remaining in union with Him?!

Perhaps in this question there is a prophecy of the Jews' acceptance of the Lord Christ in the last days, for there comes a day in which the Jews will realize that they err in seeking an earthly kingdom and temporal ambitions, whereas the need is for eternal salvation and a tasting of God's heavenly love!

entries.section: Mutual married love

paragraphs.text: 1. The bride praises her Bridegroom. 2. The dialogue of the garden. 3. A description of the bride "Shulamite."

entries.section: The bride praises her Bridegroom

paragraphs.text: When the world discovers in the bride her love for her Bridegroom and realizes the effectiveness of this love in her inner life and its reflections on her features, her feelings, and her conduct, it asks about this unique Bridegroom. Here the bride bears witness to her Bridegroom not by words but by the life she lives, for she knows Him fully and touches Him, being united with Him; He brings her into the knowledge of the invisible Father... She bears true and practical witness, saying of Him: 1. "My beloved (my friend) is white and ruddy" [10].

How sweet is this Savior-Bridegroom, for in Him the two colors, white and red, are joined, each making the other clear and complete! He is white, but not the pale white that is lifeless, like Ananias the high priest, of whom the Apostle Paul said: "God shall smite thee, thou whited wall: for sittest thou to judge me after the law, and commandest me to be smitten contrary to the law?" (Acts 23:3); for by his violation of the commandment and the Law he came under the sentence of death without life, for he lost his blood, the sign of life, and became pale like the dead; but the Savior of the Church in His whiteness bears a constant redness, a sign of perfection of strength, life, and vitality! Likewise the Savior does not bear redness apart from whiteness, otherwise there would be in that an indication of killing and bloodshed, as in the book of Revelation (Rev 6:4), and as sin is described as scarlet and red like crimson (Isa 1:18); but He is "he that cometh from Edom, with red garments from Bozrah, this that is glorious in his apparel... I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save" (Isa 63:1).

The word "white" here came in the sense of "radiant," for He is the Sun of Righteousness who shone upon us who sit in darkness, to bring us by His Holy Spirit into the fullness of the light of the knowledge of the Father. We were carried in Him through His radiance in the merits of His blood (the red), to be in the bosom of the Father and know the fullness of His mysteries. Thus His radiance is mingled with His saving work, that is, His whiteness with His redness, so that we may bear the reflections of His radiance in us by our entering to His Father.

In the book of Daniel we see His clothing white as snow (Dan 7:2), and at His Transfiguration also "his raiment was white as the light" (Mt 17:2). And what is the garment of the Lord Christ but His Church, in which He wraps Himself like a garment, dwelling within her? So the radiance and whiteness He bears He reflects on His Church, as on the heavenly ones who are in His presence always (Mk 16:5; Acts 1:10), so that we appear in heaven in white garments (Rev 3:4; 7:9), as we are enjoined thus: "Let thy garments be always white" (Eccl 9:8).

Holy Scripture speaks of many appearances of angels but does not go into describing their garments; yet in the events of the Resurrection and the Ascension Scripture assures us that the angels appeared in white garments. They appeared for our sake, that we may know that through the Lord's resurrection and ascension we are washed and made whiter than snow (Ps 50). If our sins were like scarlet - they were buried in the tomb - the Lord raised us up like snow (Isa 1:18); therefore the prophet Daniel says: "Ye shall be purified and made white" (Dan 11:35).

Thus the Church sees her Bridegroom and rejoices in His radiance and is glad in His blood... but the enemy Satan trembles before the radiance of the Savior and fears the blood of His Cross; therefore the Church says: 2. "A banner among ten thousand" [10].

He became known to men and demons: the Church knows Him as "standing for an ensign of the people" (Isa 11:10); He was lifted up on the Cross and drew humanity to Himself, to pour His radiance on it and sanctify it with blood; and the demons know Him and cry out: "Come down from the cross," because He destroyed their kingdom and made a public show of them, triumphing over them (Col 2:15).

entries.section: The bride praises her Bridegroom

paragraphs.text: 3. "His head is fine gold (pure), His locks are flowing, black as a raven" [11].

If gold signifies heavenly life, then "pure gold" signifies His divinity, for in Him "dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily" (Col 2:9). The Father appointed Him head of the Church, "from which all the body by joints and bands" (Col 2:9), for He alone, as the Son of God and His Word, is able to bring the whole body into heaven. If the head is heavenly, the body cannot live except on a heavenly level as long as the body is united with the head. This is the secret of her love for her Bridegroom, that He brings her into the heavens, that is, into the bosom of His Father, through her union with Him.

As for His flowing hair that surrounds the Church, it is the Church, or as St. Augustine says: [It is the company of the saints, who are like the hair of the Lord; not one of them falls without the permission of His Father... they live by Him. Therefore no white hair appears in Him, but He is entirely "black as a raven"; no believer grows old, but renews his youth like the eagle].
This is the work of the Holy Spirit, who grants fellowship between the members and the Head, so the members remain in the fullness of their strength through the Head, who never weakens at all.

Just as the Lord Christ is "the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever" (Heb 12:8), so His Church passes through Him beyond the bounds of time, so that old age does not touch her, nor do earthly events prevail against her!

entries.section: The bride praises her Bridegroom

paragraphs.text: 4. "His eyes are as the eyes of doves by the rivers of waters, washed with milk, sitting in their sockets (by the streams)" [12].

Though He is the awesome King who frightens the enemies, with eyes like a flame of fire (Rev 1:14), searching the details of things and their hidden parts, yet when He appears to His believers they see His eyes like the simple, gentle dove, full of innocence. His eyes are like the eyes of the dove, "of purer eyes than to behold evil" (Hab 1:13).

Father Victorinus, bishop of Pateu, a man of the third century, sees that the waters signify the many diverse peoples who came to God through Baptism; thus the speech about His eyes being like doves by the rivers of waters signifies the Lord's Incarnation and the declaration of the beginning of a new holy generation through His baptism.

As for their being washed in milk, this signifies the Lord's concern to offer His believers pure, unadulterated faith as nourishment for their souls, for St. Ambrose says: [The Lord is baptized in milk, that is, He is baptized in sincerity, and those baptized in milk are those who have the faith without defilement].

As for their sitting in their sockets, that is, their resting in their place, it signifies God's care for His Church and His children; He fixes His divine gaze on every member, and does not turn His eyes from him until He brings him into the fellowship of the glories.

We can also say that the eyes of Christ are His priests and servants, those who bear the look of Christ toward humanity, who have spiritual insight opened by the Holy Spirit as "by the Dove," to bring peoples into the waters of Baptism, where they are washed of their sins and enjoy unadulterated faith like milk. These workers sit in their sockets, that is, they have a place in the Head, "Christ," so that through Him they can look upon every soul, concerned for the salvation of all. Their likening to the eyes of Christ is scriptural, for in the Old Testament the prophet was known as the seer (Amos 7:12), since the prophet by the spirit of prophecy can see what the people cannot see. He was sometimes called the watchman (Ezek 3:17; 23:7), who stands on the tower to see whether there are enemies and warns the people.

entries.section: The bride praises her Bridegroom

paragraphs.text: 5. "His cheeks are like a thicket (bowl) of spice, and beds (overflowing) of fragrant herbs" [13].

The cheeks of the Lord Christ, which refer to His countenance, were exposed to mockery and contempt, as Isaiah the prophet says: "I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and disgrace" (Isa 50:6)... This face, which the Lord did not turn away from the spitting of the wicked (Mt 27:3), the Church sees bearing signs of self-giving love, so it is likened to a thicket of spice, that is, a group of interwoven shrubs that diffuse a sweet fragrance, and to beds (bouquets) of fragrant herbs, which the soul smells as a fragrance of life. 6. "His lips are lilies, dropping flowing myrrh" [13].

We spoke before about the Bridegroom as the lily of the wilderness, and that by union with Him believers also become lilies. But here the lips of the Bridegroom are likened to lilies (the lily flower)... What does this mean?

The lily signifies royal glory, for the Lord speaks of it, saying: "even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these" (Mt 6:29). So the lips of the Lord Christ proclaim glorious teachings, or in other words offer the word of life that is able to bring the believer into the glorious eternal life. Therefore the psalmist says of Him: "grace is poured upon His lips" (Ps 45:2).

These lips bear a fragrant perfume that drops like myrrh. The Evangelists described the words that came from them thus: "Never man spake like this man" (Jn 7:47), "And all bare him witness, and wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth. And they said, Is not this Joseph's son?" (Lk 4:22).

As for describing them as dropping myrrh mingled with liquid myrrh, it means that His words are mingled with entering into the bitterness of His sufferings and being buried with Him, since He was shrouded with liquid myrrh... Everyone who hears Him longs to enter with Him into the fellowship of His sufferings and to die with Him. As St. Gregory of Nyssa says: [Myrrh pours forth from His body and fills the souls of those who received Him, and this is a clear symbol of the mortification of the body...].

St. Gregory also sees that this mouth overflowing with lilies and flowing myrrh represents the Apostles, who are the mouth of the Lord, witnessing by the word of His Gospel, which is the lily, and bringing believers into the flowing myrrh, that is, fidelity in Baptism, or burial with Him, that they may receive the power of His resurrection. The Apostle Peter poured out a radiant lily, which is the Word, in the house of Cornelius, filling the souls of his hearers with myrrh, for they were buried with the Lord Christ in Baptism and became dead to the world.

entries.section: 7. "His hands are rings of gold set with beryl" [14].

paragraphs.text: The "ring" or "circle" signifies eternity, because it has no starting point and no end point. His hands are eternal, satisfying soul and body together forever. As for their being of gold, this is a reference to their heavenly character... For He takes hold of His bride and puts her hand in His heavenly hand to pour out His work in her, so that she bears His heavenly power and potentialities, to cross with Him to heaven.

As for the beryl, it appears repeatedly in the Old Testament (Ezek 1:16; Dan 10:6), to signify the power of founding... for "the works of his hands are verity and judgment," and both hands establish His bride on firm faith and truth.

entries.section: 8. "His belly is white ivory overlaid with blue sapphire" [14].

paragraphs.text: The belly, or the bowels, signifies God's deep feelings, full of love and tenderness, as in Jeremiah: "my bowels are troubled for him; I will surely have mercy upon him, saith the LORD" (Jer 31:20). As for this tenderness being like white ivory, it is because ivory comes as the fruit of suffering, for it is taken from the elephant through its sufferings unto death. And as for His bowels being overlaid with blue sapphire, a heavenly color, it is to declare that His love is not earthly and temporary but heavenly and eternal.

entries.section: 9. "His legs are pillars of marble set upon sockets of fine gold (gold)" [15].

paragraphs.text: The legs signify the ability to walk steadily, and the gold or fine gold signifies the heavenly nature, as though whoever is united with the Bridegroom is able to walk with Him in continual movement toward heaven, trampling beneath his feet all the powers of the devil, shattering death and conquering sin.

St. Ambrose has a beautiful comment on this phrase, for he says: [His legs are pillars of marble set upon sockets of gold, because Christ walks in souls, and makes for Himself ways in the minds of His saints, so that it is in them as though they were two bases of gold and foundations of precious stones, upon which are imprinted the footprints of the heavenly Word of God].

entries.section: 10. "His countenance is like Lebanon, a youth like the cedar" [15].

paragraphs.text: Lebanon is a beautiful tourist region to which some newlyweds resort to begin their married life in a beautiful atmosphere; so too the face of the Lord Jesus, with the cheerfulness and tenderness it bears, gladdens the soul that wants to live the spiritual married life with the divine Word. The psalmist described the Messiah, saying: "Thou art fairer than the children of men," and in the report which Pontius Pilate wrote to Herod about the Lord Christ it came: "you long to look upon Him."

As for the secret of His beauty, it lies in His being "a youth like the cedar," known for its towering height together with its uprightness and its sweet scent... Thus the Lord Christ appears to the soul as the youth who never grows old.

And the wonder is that the Lord in His condescension took on our humanity, sharing with us all the stages of growth except old age: He became an embryo among embryos, and a child among children, a boy and a youth and then a man, but He ascended before old age, for it was not fitting for Him to grow old, lest His Church bear the spirit of weakness and spiritual old age. For it came in the divine inspiration: "thy youth is renewed like the eagle's" (Ps 103:5). And it came in the rite of the Church concerning the Church and the Virgin Mary, as the ideal member of the Church: "the vine that does not grow old"...

The Christian never knows old age at all, but grows younger with the days, for though his outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16), and as the Apostle Paul says: "ye have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him" (Col 3:10)... Truly, the body weakens and may grow old, but the spirit remains active and strong (Mt 26:41; Mk 14:38).

entries.section: This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem" [16].

paragraphs.text: The psalmist says: "How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth" (Ps 119:103). So the believer finds in the words of the Lord a special sweetness and delight, because these words are spirit and life. He who eats of them returns to the Lord hungry for Him, and he who drinks of Him thirsts for Him all the more...

When man listens to the words of the Lord his heart is drawn with greater longing to know these divine mysteries, and he remains all his life sitting at the feet of the Lord, not wanting to leave Him, saying with the psalmist: "I have seen an end of all perfection: but thy commandment is exceeding broad" (Ps 119).

The secret of the sweetness of His words is that they carry power and authority, for He does not give mere commandments or advice and guidance or warnings, but gives with the word the power to carry it out, so that the commandment lifts man to enter into the knowledge of the mysteries of heaven, and the soul goes from glory to glory, continually bearing the secret of a new power that never ends.

Finally, since the bride feels the inability of language to describe her Bridegroom, she says: "He is altogether lovely." This is her Beloved, the Friend whom she seeks and strives after... He satisfies her; in Him she finds all her love, and to Him is all her longing!
When the soul bears witness to her Bridegroom, unbelievers begin to ask:
"Whither is thy beloved gone, O thou fairest among women?
Whither is thy beloved turned aside? that we may seek him with thee" [1].

Since the soul's testimony about the Bridegroom bore the reflections of His glory on her life and conduct, they called her "the fairest among women." Even the sight of her in her spiritual beauty generated in them a special attraction, not that they might cling to her in herself, but to search for her Bridegroom, who is the secret of her beauty!

They came into intense longing for Him together with perplexity, and they asked: "Where has your Beloved gone? Where did He turn? Where has He hidden? We want to know Him with you, and to go in to Him, not without you." The unbelievers realized that they cannot get to know this Bridegroom outside the Church, but with her and through her, that He is the Bridegroom of the Church; therefore in order to go in to Him it is fitting for them to accept membership in the Church... Thus He becomes a head for them. For without the Church the world does not know Christ, and outside Christ there is no Church.
As for the Church's answer, it is:
"My beloved is gone down into his garden, to the beds of spices, to feed in the gardens, and to gather lilies.
I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine: the Shepherd among the lilies" [2-3].

It is not strange that this book contains continual assurances of the presence of the Bridegroom within the Church, and His presence within the soul that He acquired with His blood. For He enters the barren stony heart and makes of it a garden for Himself (Song 4:12, 16; 5:1), indeed inner gardens in which He feeds, and there He gathers the lilies that bear the features of the Bridegroom Himself, who was also called the lily (Song 2:1).

It is as though the bride here warns against wasting time searching for the Bridegroom outside, for in His humility He came down to His Church and entered the hearts of His people. Therefore the Apostle says: "Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven? (that is, to bring Christ down)... The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart" (Rom 10:7-8).

Furthermore, in the bride's answer there is a clarification, for those outside, of the secret of the relationship between the soul and God: if God has entered into His garden to gather lilies, He does not do so as one who exploits His creation or as a lover of domination and taking, but He entered in response to a call of love issued to Him from her, for she says to Him, "I am my beloved's." As though she says: All that is mine is my Beloved's, let Him enter my heart and receive the whole heart and all the inner energies and feelings, for what I possess is His. And this call is nothing but a response to the work of love which He showed her, since "my beloved is mine." He gave me His life... and here I return His love with love! I love Him with the fullness of my choice, since He loved me with the fullness of His freedom.

As for her saying "gone down," it means her declaration of the truth of the situation, that the Bridegroom's coming down to her heart is not out of need on His part nor for humiliation, but is a condescension from Him to accept my invitation to come down into my life, that He may raise me up with Him to His heavens, taking me wholly as He gave me Himself.

He has come down into my heart... so what shall I ask? It is not fitting for me to ask of Him anything but to take Him Himself, and nothing but this request suffices me or satisfies my soul. For no earthly reward nor gifts or presents can quench my thirst, but I ask for Him... "my beloved is mine."

entries.section: The Bridegroom's conversation with His bride in the garden:

paragraphs.text: 1. "Thou art beautiful, O my love, as Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army with banners (in order)" [4].

When the bride enters into a relationship of union with her Bridegroom, each speaks intimately to the other. And now, since the bride has declared to the unbelievers and testified that He is within her in His garden, and asks them not to search for Him outside, the Bridegroom praises her, using some of the earlier expressions (Song 4) while revealing a deeper beauty, delighted by her entering into a deeper union with Him.

Here He sees her "beautiful as Tirzah." The word "Tirzah" in Hebrew means "delight or joy." And Tirzah is the youngest of the five daughters of Zelophehad the son of Hepher (Num 26:33); these daughters, whose father had died and who had no brother, stood before Moses and Eleazar the priest and before the princes and all the congregation by the door of the tabernacle of the congregation and asked to inherit their father's property with their father's brothers, and the Lord gave them this right and it became a statute of judgment (Num 27:1-11), and they also received their portion at the division of the land by Joshua the son of Nun (Josh 17:3-6). Perhaps in the Song of Songs the bride is likened to Tirzah as the youngest of the daughters who claimed their right before Moses the prophet and Joshua, and the command was issued from the Lord that they receive an inheritance and portion. This is the beauty of the soul united with Christ Jesus, that she in boldness without fear asks for her inheritance and portion, that is, her right to live as a living member in the holy congregation. And what is this inheritance or this portion that belongs to the believer but the Lord Himself, whom the soul receives within her as the secret of her glory and wealth.

And perhaps by "Tirzah" is meant the exceedingly beautiful city that originally belonged to the Canaanites, which Joshua the son of Nun took (Josh 12:24) and gave to the tribes of the children of Israel. It was the capital of the kingdom of Israel (the ten tribes) for about fifty years (1 Kgs 14:17; 15:21, 31; 16:6, 23) until Omri built Samaria. The secret of its beauty was that it had formerly been Gentile and idolatrous, but when the true Joshua reigned over it, it became the possession of the Lord.

And the Lord also sees her "comely as Jerusalem"; the secret of her comeliness is that she is like Jerusalem, the city of the King. That is, the Church has come to represent the heavenly sanctuaries in which God dwells, and the capital of the sphere of His kingdom, in which everything is beautiful and radiant.

Her beauty like Tirzah's or her comeliness like Jerusalem's has been mingled with strength, for she is "terrible as an army with banners (in order)," terrible before the enemies, because the victorious Lord in her midst protects her; she is like a heavenly army bearing the banners (flags) of victory and triumph, knowing neither defeat nor despair but the spirit of victory and strength. And according to the Greek translation, she is like an army well ordered, since its Commander is the Lord Himself.

entries.section: The Bridegroom's conversation with His bride in the garden:

paragraphs.text: In other words, the Christian bears strength together with beauty, being beautiful in his meekness and gentleness as well as strong in his courage and firmness. He is beautiful in his inner calm and mighty in his striving against sin unto blood. And the secret of his strength and victory is the "tears" which he pours out with a broken heart before God, which captivate the divine love, as the Lord says to him:
"Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me" [5].

The mercies of God were overcome by the tears of the sinful woman and the sighs of the right-hand thief. For God cannot bear to see man's tears and contrition, and perhaps the greatest example of this is Ahab the wicked king, who killed and also inherited (1 Kgs 21:19), of whom Scripture testified: "But there was none like unto Ahab, which did sell himself to work wickedness in the sight of the LORD, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up. And he did very abominably in following idols..." (1 Kgs 21:25-26); when he heard the word of the Lord against him by the mouth of Elijah the prophet he rent his clothes and put sackcloth upon his flesh and lay in sackcloth and went softly; the Lord could not bear this sight but said to Elijah the prophet: "Seest thou how Ahab humbleth himself before me? because he humbleth himself before me, I will not bring the evil in his days" (1 Kgs 21:29).

entries.section: The Bridegroom's conversation with His bride in the garden:

paragraphs.text: 2. "Thy hair is as a flock of goats lying down in Gilead. Thy teeth are as a flock of sheep which come up from the washing, whereof every one beareth twins, and there is not one barren among them, (thy lips are like a thread of scarlet, thy speech is sweet), thy cheek is like a piece of a pomegranate (seen) within thy veil" [5-7].

He had already praised her with the same attributes in chapter four (1-3), which we have already treated in some detail. As for the secret of His repeating the same expressions, it is to confirm an important truth, that God's love for man remains unchanging. For in spite of the lukewarmness man suffered - as came in chapter five - yet when she returned to Him with the tears of repentance she found Him praising her with the same expressions with which He had praised her before, and His look toward her had not changed, but His love for her increases. Perhaps this reminds us of God's dealings with the Apostle Peter, to whom, even after his denial, the Lord affirmed three times his acceptance in the apostolic work, saying to him: "Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?... Feed my sheep!" As though God's love does not change, but it depends on our love, which changes... His divine arms are still open with love.

entries.section: The Bridegroom's conversation with His bride in the garden:

paragraphs.text: 3. "There are threescore queens, and fourscore concubines, and virgins without number. One is my dove, my perfect one;
she is the only one of her mother, she is the choice one (the chosen) of her that bare her.
The daughters saw her, and blessed her; the queens and the concubines, and they praised her" [8-9].
He praises her through the language of numbers... So what does He mean by the sixty queens? And the eighty concubines? And the virgins without number? And His one perfect dove?!

First: perhaps He compared her with the heavenly creation that loves Him, and saw the heavenly ones as many orders, whom He likened to the sixty queens and the eighty concubines and the virgins without number... These are of varying degrees as to stature, but His Church, which the Bridegroom acquired with His blood and sanctified by His Holy Spirit, has become the one bride, the perfect dove... This is the secret of her beauty and perfection and strength: she has become the one Body of the Lord, though she comprises many members, for He "gathers together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad" (Jn 11:52), gathered together in Him (Eph 1:10).

As for the secret of her unity, it does not consist merely in the members' gathering together in one place, or their uniting in one language or one culture... but consists in the following divine factors:

a. She is His dove... If there is one Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of the Father and the Son together, then He gave His Church this divine Spirit to set believers in motion as one dove, receiving the life of fellowship with God. This is the work of the Holy Spirit: He grants believers fellowship with God and with one another, for since by Him we are reconciled with the Father in the merits of the blood of the Son, we receive in Baptism the Spirit of adoption by which we cry "Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15). Through this reconciliation we see ourselves members one of another.
We quote here some words of the Fathers in this matter:
* By the Holy Spirit, who gathers the people of God into one, the evil spirit, divided against itself, is driven out.

* It belongs to the Holy Spirit to give the fellowship by which we have become one body of the one only Son of God, for it is written: "If there be therefore any consolation in Christ, if any comfort of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit" (Phil 2:1).
St. Augustine * When the Most High came down and confused the tongues, He divided the nations.
But when He distributed the tongues of fire (the Holy Spirit) He called all to unity; therefore with one accord we glorify the all-holy Spirit.

entries.section: The hymn Kontakon for the feast of Pentecost

paragraphs.text: (In the Greek Orthodox Church)

b. She is His perfect one: since the Church puts on the perfect Lord Christ, she becomes perfect through Him, and her unity is based on entering into the "new perfect life" that we have in Christ Jesus. In this new life we are not subject to the law of schism or the spirit of enmity, but rather to the spirit of love, which grants inner unity. Thus our unity comes through our sanctification by union with the Holy One, so that we imitate the unity of the Holy Trinity... This is what appears clearly in the Lord's farewell prayer, on the night of His passion, when He says:
"Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we are.
That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee,
that they also may be one...
I in them, and thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one" (Jn 17).
Regarding this the martyr St. Cyprian says: [This is what He longed for us: that we live in the same pattern of unity that exists between the Father and the Son in their being one].

And St. Cyril of Alexandria says: [He desires for us a union with one another after the same pattern as the unity of the Holy Trinity... this unity, which is the most perfect union, must be reflected in the unity of the believers].

c. The only one of her mother and the chosen of her that bare her: Who is this mother or this bearer who looks upon the Church as her only one and chosen one?! It is the heavenly Jerusalem, whose work is nothing but waiting for this one bride whom the Lord Jesus betrothed, to remain a partner in glory forever. As though the secret of unity springs from the believers' entering into eternity... or their departure from the sphere of time. For if our temporal life breeds the spirit of schism and jealousy, then our enjoyment of the pledge of the heavenly things grants us love toward all humanity and longing on an eternal level. For the law of heaven is peace and unity, and its language is love.

The Bridegroom says: "The daughters saw her, and blessed her; the queens and the concubines, and they praised her," that is, the heavenly ones bless her, for they see that she has submitted to their law and spoken their language, and has become one of them and not a stranger to them.
Second: the language of the symbolic numbers can be understood as declarations about the secret of the Church's beauty, perfection, and strength:

a. Sixty queens: the Church is likened to sixty queens, because if the number 12 represents the kingdom of God on earth, as we saw before, since the Holy Trinity reigns over the four quarters of the world (3 x 4), then since God reigns over the five senses of believers (12 x 5), the number sixty is a symbol of God's kingship over the life of believers, or over the life of the Church extended to all the quarters of the world. Thus the Church becomes sixty queens... the King of kings reigns in us, so our life is not in slavery but rises to bear royal glory.

b. Eighty concubines: in the first number the Church appeared as a queen through God's reign over her senses, but here the Church appears as a concubine, that is, living a hidden spiritual life with the Bridegroom. As for the number eighty, it signifies the Church's being marked with the eschatological nature while still on earth. For the number 10 signifies our temporal life, therefore the Ten Commandments came in the Old Testament as a divine law that we practice on earth, but the number 8 (10 x 8) signifies the other life, as we saw before, because it exceeds the number 7, which signifies the week of our life. Therefore circumcision came on the eighth day, and the Lord rose on the first day of the new week, or the eighth of the previous week, and eight souls were saved in Noah's ark... all of these signify the new upper or heavenly life. So the Church, while living on earth (10), lives the new heavenly life (8).

c. Virgins without number: this unlimited number signifies the virginity of the whole life for the Lord, so the believer offers a virgin heart that accepts no bridegroom other than the Lord, and a virgin mind that thinks only of the things of the Lord, and virgin feelings... therefore the kingdom of God was likened to virgins who went out to meet the bridegroom.

d. The one: the oneness of the Church is a principal feature in the life of the Church, for the believer declares "We believe in one holy catholic apostolic Church," and we have already seen the secret of this oneness...
Her sonship to the one God the Father by her union with Christ through the Holy Spirit in Baptism.

St. Irenaeus sees that the secret of this unity is also "the unity of faith," for he says: [The true Church, which is truly ancient, is one Church... The early catholic Church alone works in the unity of the faith].

And in Father Rufinus' discourse on the Apostles' Creed he mentioned this phrase (Song 6:9), explaining that the secret of this unity is the one faith, for he says: [Whoever receives this faith in the Church, let him not go outside to vain counsel, nor take part with workers of iniquity].
