paragraphs.text: And we can understand "My dove, my perfect one, is but one" to be St. Mary the Virgin, for many received honor, but she surpassed them all, and it came in the Sunday Theotokia:
"Hail to you, O Mary, the beautiful dove, who bore for us God the Word"

And what is mentioned in the Song afterward applies to her: "Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, pure as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners (in order)?" [10]. She is radiant as the morning, for from her became incarnate the Sun of Righteousness, who shone on us who sat in darkness for a time. And she is fair as the moon, deriving her beauty from the light of her Son. Pure or chosen as the sun, for the Holy Spirit came upon her, who purified her and prepared her for the divine Incarnation. Terrible as an army in order, for she bears within her the Lord of hosts, the Commander of the battle against sin and the kingdom of the devil.

We can also understand the text in another way, for every soul that meets with God and bears His Holy Spirit within her through the Church and puts on Christ Jesus, the Lord calls her by her name, and shines in her with His light, so she becomes radiant without darkness, fair as the moon, chosen and beautiful by His blood, terrible and victorious by His Cross.

entries.section: The bride's concern for work:

paragraphs.text: "I went down into the garden of nuts to see the greens of the valley, and to see whether the vine flourished,
and whether the pomegranates budded?
There will I give thee my breasts. I did not perceive until my soul had made me like the chariots of Amminadab (a noble people).
Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee.
What will ye see in the Shulamite?
Like the ordering of ranks in a camp (like the dance of two ranks)" [11-13].

If the Lord has praised His bride thus, the bride, before this great love, did not stand to listen to the praise but went down to her inner valley to work, went down to the garden of nuts and gave attention to the vine and the pomegranate tree.

What does the garden of nuts mean? The scholar Origen answers: [The bride went down to the garden of nuts to discover that the nut had put forth its fruit in a priestly way], for the rod of Aaron the high priest budded and bore the fruit of nuts (Num 17:8).

And the nut in truth represents the word of God, which occupies the heart of the priest continually, offering it as a rich table for his people to eat and be satisfied and bear much fruit. When the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah the priest, he was asked: "What seest thou, Jeremiah?" And he said: "I see a rod of an almond tree," then the Lord said to him: "Thou hast well seen: for I am watching over my word to perform it" (Jer 1:11-12).

And the scholar Origen explains the use of the "nut" as a symbol of the word of God by saying that the nut has a bitter outer covering, the husk, which dries and falls off, then the thick inner covering, which is broken so that man may eat the sweet inner fruit. Thus the scholar sees that the word of God has the bitter literal interpretation which the Jews used, then the moral or behavioral interpretation, which is like the thick shell, where it drives man to a life of faithfulness (the breaking), striving unto blood, to enter into the sweet spiritual meaning, which is granted as food for the spiritual, by which they live not only in this world but also in the next world.

Therefore behold, the soul has gone down into her inner depths as into the garden of the word of God working in her; there she sees the fruits of the valley. There in the heart she perceives the spiritual meanings of the word that satisfy her, as though she says to the Bridegroom: If You have praised me thus, I have no merit, but it is the fruit of Your divine word planted within me by Your divine hand.

And the wonder is that the Lord's praise of the faithful soul does not drive her to pride but pricks her to work, so she goes down to see the Lord's vineyard that is within her and the trees which His right hand planted: has the vine flowered?! Have the pomegranates blossomed?!

When she enters the garden of the Lord within her and touches His work in her, she rejoices in the fruit even though it is still at the beginning, and speaks intimately with her Bridegroom: "There will I give thee my breasts"... as though she says to Him: I return Your love with love. You offered me Your breasts, which are the Old Testament and the New Testament, and behold Your word has borne fruit within me, so I return to You what is Yours: I give You my breasts, that is, I offer You the same two Testaments. For Your book has become my book! But how does she offer Him these two breasts? When she bears practical witness to the word of God before others and offers the word to her brethren, she has offered it to the Bridegroom Himself... as He says: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me" (Mt 25:40).

Though she sees in the vine only a flower and in the pomegranate also its "blossom," she perceived that God had made her soul like the chariots of Amminadab or the chariots of a noble people. For the word "Amminadab" means "my people are noble." By the power of the word she has become the honored people of God, fighting and striving to the end against sin.

Her view of herself as the chariots of Amminadab carried other meanings also, among them: 1. Amminadab the father of Nahshon (Ruth 4:19; Ex 6:23) of the tribe of Judah, from whose seed came the Lord Christ; so the secret of her honor is her belonging to the King Christ, the true Commander of the chariots, by whom we conquer completely. 2. Another Amminadab of the sons of Uzziel, a Levite, one of the chiefs whom King David chose to carry the ark of the covenant (1 Chr 15:3, 10)... as though the soul has been granted in the New Testament to carry Christ Himself within her... this is the secret of her fruitfulness and sanctification. 3. Amminadab the son of Kohath, also of the Levites (1 Chr 6:24)... whom David the prophet appointed with others to sing or praise in the house of the Lord after the ark came to rest (1 Chr 6:31)... as though this is the work of the soul united with Christ Jesus her Bridegroom: "continual praise."
So the Church, or the soul as a member of the Church, finds herself in a state of striving and warfare under the leadership of the Bridegroom, sanctified by Him, praising Him and thanking Him!
In this atmosphere full of striving with joy and praise the Bridegroom calls His bride, saying:
"Return, return, O Shulamite.

entries.section: The bride's concern for work:

paragraphs.text: Return, return, that we may look upon thee." [13].

He called her "Shulamite," which is the feminine of "Shalem or Salem or Solomon," as though the Lord Christ, who is the true Solomon, calls her by His own title. She bore His person within her, and His traits in her conduct, and His name was called upon her.

He looks at her while she is in a state of war and calls her "Shulamite," that is, the bearer of peace! And the secret of her peace is her continual return to Him... and that the Holy Trinity looks at her and cares for her and does not forget her... "Return, return, that we may look upon thee."
He returns and looks at those around Him, saying:
What will ye see in the Shulamite?!
Like the ordering of ranks in a camp (like the dance of two ranks)" [13].

The Lord Christ takes pride in His Church, or in the soul that is a member of His Church, for He sees her, bearing peace within her, as having become like ordered ranks of soldiers for spiritual warfare!

And according to the Hebrew text He sees her as "the dance of two ranks"; the word "two ranks" means "two armies." As though the Lord declares that His Church has borne the dances of the two armies as a sign of victory and triumph. This reminds us of the dances of joy performed by Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, with the rest of the women, as they praised the Lord who delivered them from Pharaoh and his army (Ex 15:20). And also when David the prophet killed Goliath the giant, the women came out of all the cities singing and dancing (1 Sam 18:6).

entries.section: 1. "How beautiful are thy steps (thy feet) with shoes, O prince's daughter!" [1].

paragraphs.text: He calls her "prince's daughter" since she is related to God, born of water and the Spirit as a daughter of the heavenly King. Therefore she was called in the psalm (Ps 45:13) "the king's daughter." Though in her origin (after the Fall) she was lowly and despised, by her relation to God she bore a royal origin.

The bride had already praised her Bridegroom (Song 5:11-15), describing Him beginning from the head down to the feet, for she was dazzled by His majesty and glory, so she spoke of the head, which represents His person, then progressed to praise even His feet. But the Bridegroom, in praising the bride, begins with the feet, or her steps, until He describes the head, and that for two reasons: first, that He wants to confirm that the secret of her beauty is her steps, or her walking in the royal way, that is, her return in repentance to the Bridegroom, the secret of her life. And the second reason is that He wanted to give greater honor to the members that seem to be without honor (1 Cor 12:23-24).

As for His speaking of the "shoes," it refers to the Church - as a congregation or as members - having been shod with the Gospel of peace (Eph 6:15), as though the Bridegroom concentrated at the beginning of describing her on her evangelical steps... she walks the way of the Bridegroom Himself, practicing her evangelical life full of peace. This is the secret of her spiritual beauty, that she knew the way and entered it! Thus she also bears witness to her Bridegroom, as the Apostle Paul says: "How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!" (Rom 10:15). And the saying of the prophet Isaiah: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!" (Isa 52:7), and the saying of Nahum the prophet: "Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace! O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the king shall no more pass through thee" (Nah 1:15).

When the soul is shod with the word of the Lord she becomes a bearer of the secret of her inner peace and of the peace of others, so she preaches the word of salvation and proclaims the kingdom of God declared on the Cross, and pours joy into the hearts of believers; thereby they obtain the spirit of victory and triumph over the destroyer.

entries.section: 2. "The joints of thy thighs are like jewels (chains), the work of the hands of a cunning workman" [1].

paragraphs.text: The thighs carry the body and help it to move, therefore the joints of the thighs signify the unity of the holy Church in Christ Jesus through love. Regarding this the Apostle says: "speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ: from whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love" (Eph 4:15-16). Through this unity the body grows and is strengthened (Col 2:19), so the mission of the Church is accomplished.

This unity, like chains, binds humanity together despite its differences in language, race, and cultures, and also binds the generations together, so the Church bears the catholic spirit on the level of place (in all the world) and the level of time (across the generations)... and it is the work of the hands of a skilled craftsman, namely the Holy Spirit, the giver of fellowship.

entries.section: 3. "And thy navel is a round cup, which wanteth not mixed drink" [2].

paragraphs.text: The navel is signed with the oil of the Holy Myron in the sacrament of Confirmation (Chrismation), because the Holy Spirit sanctifies the outward members as He sanctifies the inward parts, so that man may be wholly the Lord's.

When the Lord spoke with Ezekiel about the ugliness to which man had come and the death that had befallen him, He said of him: "And as for thy nativity, in the day thou wast born thy navel was not cut" (Ezek 16:14). For the infant, when it comes out of its mother's womb, must have its navel cut so that it comes out into the light of new life as a living being independent of its mother, no longer needing to be nourished by her blood through the umbilical cord, but begins to practice its humanity to come out to full maturity. In the same way, when the bride and bridegroom enter married life they are bound to have the umbilical cords binding them to their fathers' houses cut, so that they may live the new married life and their mature love may be exercised in the oneness of spirit. I say, thus the Lord Christ sees in His Church that she has entered with Him into married life on a heavenly level, and has cut her navel, so she has become a round cup, that is, has borne the heavenly nature (the circle that has no beginning or end), lacking no mixed drink, for she is no longer in the bowels of the world seeking its outward joys... She has departed, as it were, from her earthly father's house to live in the inner house of the wedding in true satisfaction and sufficiency.

entries.section: 4. "Thy belly is a heap (a pile) of wheat set about with lilies" [3].

paragraphs.text: The Church contains within her storehouses of spiritual food (wheat) that satisfies the soul, in which the Lord Christ dwells, the living Bread which came down from heaven, of which whoever eats shall live forever (Jn 6:51). Thus the Church may appear outwardly poor and hungry, but her bowels are storehouses of good things that satisfy hungry souls, and as the Apostle Paul says: "as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things" (2 Cor 6:10).
These good things are surrounded by a hedge of sweet-smelling lilies, as though the fruits of the Church are satisfying and beautiful, drawing souls.

entries.section: 5. "Thy two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle" [3].

paragraphs.text: He had already described her thus in Song 4:5 (which may be consulted).

entries.section: 6. "Thy neck is as a tower of ivory" [4].

paragraphs.text: He had already described her thus: "Thy neck is like the tower of David builded for an armoury" (Song 4:4), as steadfast and strong, facing every war, but now He describes her neck as "a tower of ivory," and we have already seen that ivory signifies the acceptance of suffering unto death... for it is taken from the elephant through its sufferings unto death. If the faith of the Church is high as a tower, lifted up toward heaven, she has accepted all ranks of suffering unto death... to remain faithful in her faith, not turning aside after every wind of strange teaching and not being defiled by innovations and heresies; her genuine apostolic faith has cost her a great price!
It is a faith of ivory, brilliantly white, with nothing to mar it, and precious!
This neck also signifies the chastity and purity of the Church, for she is continually lifting up her head; sin cannot bow it down to the dust or humble her.

entries.section: 7. "Thine eyes are like the pools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim" [4].

paragraphs.text: If He had previously described her eyes as the eyes of a dove, in which appears the image of the Holy Spirit, who sanctifies her inner conduct through her continual looking to Him without deviation, He now describes them as the fishponds in Heshbon. This sight reveals the breadth of her insight, for she is like pools open to heaven, which nothing veils from her. This openness toward heaven generates in her an openness toward men also, therefore He called her "fishponds"; everyone who looks at her finds that she contains the fishes within her... not concerned with the things of herself but with those of others (the fishes signify the company of believers)...

He does not describe her as springs lest they bear bubbles of air (which signify the hollow life), nor as the sea, for there are no disturbances or anxiety in her, but in the simplicity of faith she lives with a calm spiritual gaze.
As for the choice of the city of Heshbon, it is for many reasons, among them:
a. "Heshbon" means "reckoning"... So the broad and simple outlook does not mean that man lives without reckoning or without care... but with wisdom he takes into account the counting of the cost.

b. The city of Heshbon, now called "Hesban," is the ruins of a city standing on an isolated hill about 16 miles east of the Jordan and about nine miles north of Medeba, standing between the Arnon and the Jabbok. This city was taken by Sihon king of the Amorites as the capital of his kingdom and Moses the prophet gave it to the Reubenites, and it lies on the border dividing the possessions of Reuben and Gad (Num 32:37; Josh 13:26). It is one of the six cities of refuge of the 48 cities given to the Levites (Josh 21:37; 1 Chr 6:66). As though the eyes of the Church or the spiritual insight of the believer are like the calm pools in one of the cities of refuge, to which people flee and enjoy Christ Jesus, the true refuge.

c. The city of Heshbon was at the crossroads of the main roads, many multitudes passing through it, and here is a reference to the opening of the believer's heart to many, that they may enjoy the Lord Christ, "the eternal refuge." Therefore the Bridegroom completes His speech, saying: "by the gate of Bath-rabbim." The bath is a unit of measure among the Jews used for liquids, and "rabbim" means "daughter of the multitudes"... as though the believer becomes a son of many multitudes. Or as though man, having enjoyed spiritual insight, calls the multitudes to share this insight with him.

entries.section: 8. "Thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon which looketh toward Damascus" [4].

paragraphs.text: This expression signifies the nobility of the Church and her holy courage in the truth, and her not fearing falsehood, for though she is meek and humble, she is at the same time strong and mighty.

And the nose also signifies the sense of smell for distinguishing between the sweet fragrance of Christ and the passing perfumes of the world. The true believer has a nose like a tower, through which he discerns who is enemy and who is friend, and distinguishes what is for edification and what is for destruction. As for its direction toward Damascus, the commercial city concerned with temporal things, it signifies the boldness of the Church and her ability to face every current.

If the believer is bound to have such a nose, how much more is it fitting that the shepherd not be "flat-nosed" (Lev 21:7-21). And as Pope Gregory (the Great) says: [The flat-nosed is he who is unable to discern, for by the sense of smell we distinguish sweet scents from foul. This sense truly signifies the sense of discernment by which we choose virtue and reject vice. Therefore it was said in praise of the Church the bride: "Thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon." For the holy Church perceives fully by discernment the trials raised against her for various reasons, and knows beforehand - from above her tower - the battles of evil that are about to occur].

entries.section: 9. "Thine head upon thee is like Carmel,

paragraphs.text: and the hair of thine head like scarlet; the king is held in the galleries" [5].

The head of the Church is lifted high like Carmel, the mountain that rises to less than 2000 feet, not in human haughtiness and arrogant self-importance, but in the power of victory over the love of the world and all its storms.

And Carmel means "garden land," distinguished by dense greenery and many fruits and forests; so the head of the Church does not appear empty but fruitful, no vain thoughts play in her, but she bears glorious works and offers fruits that satisfy many.

Mount Carmel - which was on the southern border of Asher (Josh 19:26) - brings to us glorious and effective memories. There Elijah the prophet stood before the priests of Baal and all the people, asking them not to halt between two opinions: let them serve God or Baal...! And there the priests of Baal were slain (1 Kgs 18:17-40). So when the Church is lifted up toward the heavenly things she does not know halting between the love of God and the love of the world, but kills within her every deviation from the truth, and leads all by the truth.

On the top of Carmel Elijah the prophet worshiped and fell to the earth, asking God to give rain upon the land (1 Kgs 18:42-46), and in the Church believers worship with contrition before God that He may rain upon dry hearts with the waters of His grace until they soften with repentance and bring forth the fruit required...
And his disciple Elisha the prophet visited Mount Carmel (2 Kgs 2:25), where the widow met him that he might raise her only son from the dead (2 Kgs 4:25)...

These are some of our memories on Mount Carmel, to which the head of the Church, lifted above her enemies (Ps 27:6), is likened. As for the hair, we saw before that it signifies the company of believers. It is like scarlet, which is the clothing of kings and also bears the symbol of the blood of the Lord Christ; by our union with the Bridegroom the King, all the members have come to bear the mark of royalty through their sanctification by the precious blood.

Before this beautiful, pious sight the Bridegroom says: "the king is held in the galleries," as though He does not want to leave her. This is what the psalmist affirmed by saying: "For the LORD hath chosen Zion; he hath desired it for his habitation. This is my rest for ever: here will I dwell" (Ps 132:13-14).

entries.section: 10. "How beautiful art thou and how sweet, O my beloved!

paragraphs.text: This is thy greatness in thy delights: this thy stature is like to a palm tree, and thy breasts to clusters.
I said, I will go up to the palm tree, I will take hold of the high boughs thereof.
And thy breasts shall be as clusters of the vine, and the smell of thy nose like apples.
And the roof of thy mouth like the best wine, that goeth down sweetly with delight for my beloved, and flows over my lips and my teeth" [6-9].

At the conclusion of His description of her He speaks intimately to her: How beautiful art thou?! How sweet art thou?! - according to the original text: "How beautiful hast thou become?!" For the beauty of the Bridegroom was poured out upon her; by His dwelling within her she has acquired a special sweetness! He was mingled with her fruit, which the Lord seeks and finds in her. He looked at her stature and found it like the palm tree, and her breasts like the clusters.

Behold, the stature of the Church has appeared; she is like the palm tree, distinguished by its height and uprightness... she has risen to attain the fullness of the stature of Christ (Eph 4:13). And as the psalmist says: "The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon" (Ps 92:12). Therefore the seventy apostles were symbolized by seventy palm trees (Ex 15:27; Num 33:9), and the house of God was adorned with palm trees (1 Kgs 6:29; Chr 3:5; Ezek 40:22; 41:18), and in eternity believers carry palm branches as a sign of victory (Rev 7). The palm tree with its deep hidden roots meets the springs of living water, and it presents its fruit visibly and beneficially to many, especially in desolate regions... and its branches are used in receiving kings, who wave them as a sign of conquest and victory. As though the heavenly Bridegroom sees in His Church - through her likeness to the palm tree - the hidden deep union with Him, and the fruits offered to the hungry world, and the royal life that is triumphant and victorious!

The Bridegroom rejoices in His fruitful bride, so He goes up to the palm tree to gather its fruit. He did not send one of the servants to gather the fruit for Him, but goes up Himself and picks the fruit with His hands; here He declares to the human soul her dignity and greatness, for if for her sake He came down to the world to be united with her, now He goes up upon her... She was lifted up after having been fallen, and by her rising with her Bridegroom to His heavens she shares His glories; He sees Himself going up on His palm tree gathering its fruit, which is in truth the work of His Holy Spirit!

He takes hold of its high boughs... as though He sees in her victory a victory for Himself, and in her loftiness a glorification of His saving work. We hold the branches because by the Lord we conquer and triumph. And He holds our victory because it is on His account and for the glory of His holy name. He rejoices and exults in every victory we attain!

entries.section: As for the kinds of fruit, they are:

paragraphs.text: a. He sees her breasts as clusters of the vine... and we have seen that the breasts of the Church are the Old and New Testaments, which stir the spirit of joy in the lives of the believers.
b. He sees her nose as apples... and we have seen that the apple is a symbol of the divine Incarnation, as though she continually smells the fragrance of the incarnate God.

c. Her throat like the good wine signifies words of continual joy, pleasant and delicious in taste, which make the Bridegroom Himself also rejoice at her joy, so that signs of joy appear on His lips and teeth.
When the bride heard the Bridegroom's description and His praise of her, she answered Him: All that You have described me with is from You and for You, O my Beloved.

entries.section: As for the kinds of fruit, they are:

paragraphs.text: "I am my beloved's (my near one's), and his desire is toward me" [10].

In the second chapter, when the bride looked at the Crucified One she perceived His love through which the Lord offered Himself to her as Bridegroom, and she offered her life as His possession... saying: "My beloved (my near one) is mine, and I am his: the Shepherd among the lilies" (Song 2:16).

And in the fifth chapter she asks Him to enter His garden, that is, her heart, to accept her love for Him and to receive her life with all her inner energies as a response of love to His work with her, saying: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine: the Shepherd among the lilies" (Song 6:3). But here she has risen to eternity, not to offer her life to Him in response to His love but to disclose, on the level of openness and infinity, the extent of His longing for her: "I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me." As though she says to Him... I have come to know the secret of Your praise of me, that You ask me to be with You and for You, to be the object of Your longing forever!
This time she does not say: "my beloved is mine," for she was amazed before His delight in her and His longing toward her... He "hath desired Zion for his habitation" (Ps 132:13)...

entries.section: As for the kinds of fruit, they are:

paragraphs.text: Before this love that she discovered in her Bridegroom toward her she began calling Him:

entries.section: "Come, my beloved (my near one), let us go forth into the field;

paragraphs.text: let us lodge in the villages.
Let us get up early to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine hath flowered?!
Have the tender grapes opened?!
Have the pomegranates blossomed?!
There will I give thee my love (my breasts)" [11-12].

When the bride perceived His love for her she began asking Him that they might go out together alone to the field and lodge in the villages away from the noise of the city, and gather of the fruits...

entries.section: The field:

paragraphs.text: What field is this to which she called her beloved to go out with her? Perhaps it is the field of divine work, extended over all humanity, of which the Lord Himself said: "Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest" (Jn 4:35)... If our Lord Himself calls us to work, yet we shall not go out without Him, but with Him and by Him, for He is the owner of the vineyard and He is the One who gives it increase. Regarding this the Apostle Paul says: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase. So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase... For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building" (1 Cor 3:6-9).

Cain went out to the field but not in the company of the Lord; he went out alone, and there he could not bear the righteous Abel but killed him, and when the Lord reproached him in the boldness of evil he answered: "Am I my brother's keeper?!" (Gen 4:9), and He cursed the earth with him and because of him: "And now art thou cursed from the earth, which hath opened her mouth to receive thy brother's blood from thy hand; when thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth." But the bride refuses to go out to the field except with her Bridegroom and by Him, so her heart expands with love for her brother, and she feels responsibility toward him, so the earth is blessed because of her.

And perhaps the field reminds us of the loving meeting between Isaac and his bride Rebekah, for he went out to meditate in the field at the eventide and saw his wife coming on a camel... and she, when she saw him, alighted from the camel and met him... Here the bride longs to go out with Him to the field of contemplations; there her heavenly Bridegroom discloses to her His divine secrets, and she perceives His unspeakable glories; He receives her as His bride forever and she lives in His eternal embrace.

And perhaps the bride means by the field "the life of continual striving," for the book of Proverbs says: "He that tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread" (Prov 12:11)... for the soul has no ability to strive to be satisfied unless the Lord works with her and in her.

entries.section: Going out:

paragraphs.text: The bride says: "let us go forth..."

In the Lord's speech to His bride and His praise of her she discovered a truth she had not previously perceived in its fullness... that God is not a hard idea isolated in heaven, as Aristotle said of Him that He moved the world and stopped to control it, but rather God is always in motion in His dealing with man. God is a love that is not isolated, who came out to us leaving His glories for a time so that we would not fear and dread Him but love Him and accept Him... He came out to us and dwelt among us. For our sake He became a servant! He also went out outside the camp bearing our shame on His shoulders! And here we see Him going out to us, not disclosing Himself to us that we may love Him, but declaring in us a beauty which is in truth the reflection of His beauty upon us and the fruit of His love that besieges us. And now the soul calls upon Him, saying "let us go forth...," as though she has perceived that without Him she remains a prisoner of "herself," living captive in her shell, asking only for what is for herself. It is a supplication, indeed a cry of love, in which the soul begs her Bridegroom to release her from herself to live with Him in the field of love, asking what is for others.

This is a living picture of true married life, for neither party seeks to imprison the other within himself, consuming him for his own account... but while opening the heart to bring the other into it, both go forth together in a unitive love in which each esteems the other as a living independent being. In other words, we often see one of the spouses in his love for the other asking what is for himself, and seeing in the other party not a person living with him on the level of sharing but a "thing" in which he delights, and he stifles his breath and exploits him to satisfy his psychological, social, and biological needs. In his love for the other party he smothers the other's will, freedom, and humanity... supposing that by this he loves him!

So when the bride opens her heart to the Bridegroom to enter her, she does not seek Him "to consume Him," if this expression is correct, or as St. John Chrysostom says "to exploit Him," wanting in her Bridegroom to shape Him as she wants, who responds to all her requests and satisfies all her needs and solves all her problems and merely blesses all her actions... But it is fitting that she go out from herself, go out with Him and by Him, so she asks of Him Himself first and submits to His will, and if she asks Him anything and requests a solution of her problems or a blessing for her work, it is only as a fruit of their meeting together, not as the goal of this meeting. In other words: God first in her life... she loves Him for His own sake and not on the level of benefit!

entries.section: Let us lodge in the villages:

paragraphs.text: What are these villages in which she wants to lodge with her Bridegroom?! 1. Perhaps she means by the villages her inner life with its many aspects, as though she says to Him: Come, let us go from the outward appearances of the city and enter my heart and my mind and my emotions and all my inner energies, and lodge with me there, that we may together discover the various fruits of Your Holy Spirit within me; we find the vine has flowered and the pomegranate has blossomed and my breasts offer the milk of pure love. 2. Perhaps here also is a call to serve the villages, for many care for the service of the rich city, but the bride - the Church - is bound to preach and to care within the villages, where the simple and the poor are also. 3. Here is the call to lodge with Him in "many" villages, that is, to accompany Him from village to village, and her heart does not rest in the city or in any one village, but enters with her Bridegroom into the life of union through her service in every place... So the believer does not find the fullness of his rest until his inner depths are at ease concerning all humanity. In the first chapter (Song 1:6) the soul reproached the daughters of Jerusalem that they had made her keeper of the vineyards, but now she is the one who asks to rise early to the many vineyards... She has come out of every selfishness and every closedness to rise early to the vineyards of others, working in them with the Lord, the genuine Vinedresser. And the wonder is that not only has her heart expanded to serve others, but she hastens the service: "let us get up early...". She has realized that the time is short and the days are evil (Eph 5:16).

Finally the bride says "there will I give thee my love (my breasts)"... there in the field of service, in the Lord's field, in the villages, in the vineyards, when she offers to humanity her union with Christ her Bridegroom, she is offering to the Lord her love, or offering her breasts (the two Testaments), offering the word of God as the satisfying nourishment for souls.

entries.section: Let us lodge in the villages:

paragraphs.text: Finally she says to Him:

entries.section: "The mandrakes give forth their fragrance,

paragraphs.text: and at our gates are all manner of precious things (fruits), new and old, which I have laid up for thee, O my beloved" [13].

The mandrake is one of the most beautiful flowers that signify the marital union between a man and his wife, therefore a dispute arose because of it between Rachel and Leah (Gen 30:14)... But the bride concludes her speech by saying that the fragrance of the unitive or marital love between the heavenly Bridegroom and His bride has wafted forth, and the time has come for the perfection of this union.

This union whose fragrance has appeared bears precious fruits, which come new every day and old, that is, genuine and deep... they are the fruits of the word of God working in the souls of the believers. These precious fruits appeared at the gates of the believers, who are members of the holy bride.
This is what the bride, the mother, offers to Christ the eternal Bridegroom... she offers the fruits of her members by the Holy Spirit!

At the beginning of the Song the bride began by pleading to enter into the life of fellowship with Him. She desired to be alone with Him more and more, once in the wilderness, again in the garden, a third time in the field and the villages, and a fourth time in her mother's house, to give Him to drink of the wine of her love, as He had given her to drink of His eternal love. Therefore she speaks to Him, saying:
"O that thou wert as my brother, that sucked the breasts of my mother! when I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; yea, I should not be despised.

I would lead thee, and bring thee into my mother's house, and the chamber of her that conceived me: thou wouldest instruct me: I would cause thee to drink of the mingled wine of the juice of my pomegranate" [1-2].

If this chapter is in essence a discourse about service, then the foundation of service, and its basis, is that the servant first enjoys the Bridegroom of the Church, so that when he meets his brethren they may smell in him the fragrance of "life" and receive membership in the Church, the body of the living Christ.

In this discourse we also notice the following: 1. She desires to kiss Him as a brother of hers, who sucked the breasts of her mother... For according to the ancient Eastern traditions it was not fitting to practice kisses openly even between a man and his wife, and none was excepted from this except the nearest relatives, such as parents and brothers. Therefore she wants Him as a brother of hers who sucked the breasts of her mother, so that she may take Him in her arms, appear with Him openly, and kiss Him in the presence of all mankind, and no one would blame her. 2. Perhaps the secret of her calling to Him with the hope, "O that thou wert as my brother...", is that she declares the longing of the Church of the Old Testament, which looked to God as One who is outside, for she says, "I should find thee without". She asks Him to come down to the human race and not remain isolated, but to become a firstborn brother by sharing our nature and dwelling in our midst, so that we may come to know Him, and receive Him with the kisses of open worship, and bring Him into our inner life. 3. It is also the discourse of the Church of the New Testament, who realized in the maturity of her love that the Lord Christ, the firstborn Brother, who is her Lord, her Master and her Bridegroom, is kissed by the believers with the kisses of living worship, and they bring Him into the house of their mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, to live with Him face to face in His eternal embrace. 4. As for her saying, "thou wouldest instruct me"..., it is a revelation of the nature of the true Christian and the faithful servant. For even if the soul meets her Bridegroom, kisses Him and lives with Him in her mother's house, the Church or the heavenly Jerusalem, and there gives Him to drink of the wine of her joy mingled with the juice of her pomegranate, yet she remains in humility, wanting to learn... She is in need of Him to teach her His heavenly mysteries, so that even in eternity, when she remains in His embrace, she sees Him constantly new in her eyes... as though from one moment to the next (if this expression is right, for in eternity there are no moments or time) she learns something new about His divine mysteries.

The true servant remains always in the Church, the house of his mother, at the feet of the Savior, asking to learn, even if he is called "teacher" or "father" by many! In this St. Ambrose says: [I wish to strive in learning so that I may be able to teach. For there is one Master (God) who alone does not learn what He teaches to all. But men must learn before they teach, and receive from God their Teacher what they teach others.] St. Jerome also says: [The mind that longs to learn deserves praise even if it has no teacher.] 5. Learning in the Church, the house of the mother, is not merely intellectual knowledge or memorizing teachings by heart, but in essence it is entering into the practice of "life with Christ". Therefore the bride says: "I would cause thee to drink of the mingled wine of the juice of my pomegranate"... This is what I learn: to return Your love with love. 6. When a person enters the Church in the company of the Lord, and here sits at the feet of the Savior learning, he offers wine mingled with the juice of the pomegranate... What does this mean? We have seen wine as a symbol of the life of joy and gladness... For the Church is the joyful house that receives repentant sinners, and the Lord gives them an inner joy and a gladness that temporal events cannot take away. As for the pomegranate, it signifies the life of spiritual striving, for the pomegranate tree is full of thorns, and its rind is bitter, and inside it are many seeds, but its juice carries a beautiful flavor and a delicious taste. So joy in Christianity is mingled with labors and spiritual striving to the end.
Finally the bride affirms her union with her Bridegroom and her attachment to Him, and repeats what she had said before:
"His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me.
I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes (powers) of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please" [3-4].
These are the same words that she uttered when she declared that she was "sick of love", and we have already explained them.

Perhaps she wanted to affirm here that even though she offered all her life for service, yet in this she does not stop her fellowship with Him and her preoccupation with Him... Rather, she affirms that she will not allow anything or anyone to hinder her union with Him, for living service does not distract the servant from his Christ, but in truth leads him into deeper depths of life with Him.

entries.section: The testimony of the world to Him:

paragraphs.text: As the world looks at the Church, which is the body of Christ and His witness before it, it says to her:
"Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness, all white, leaning upon her beloved (her near one)?!" [5].

The daughters of Jerusalem had already uttered similar words (Song 3:6) when they saw the wonderful change in the life of the believers. Baptism had given them a heavenly whiteness, and they enjoyed a true reliance upon the Beloved, who is able to lift them up from the wilderness of this world and bring them into His heavens. Now the world marvels through the testimony of the working bride before them... She does not amaze them merely by the abundance of her work, but rather by the fruit in her life, for the appearance of the servant in the white garments of Baptism is the best testimony for the Bridegroom...

St. Augustine comments on this text saying: [She was not white from the beginning, but became white afterwards, for "though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow" (Isa 1:18).] He also says: [Who is this that cometh up white in the splendor of light and not with a false color?!] And St. Ambrose says: [She was black before, so how did she suddenly become white (through Baptism)?!]

And St. Augustine explains the secret of her continuing whiteness thus: [Now this one who has become white walks well, because she continues leaning upon Him who made her white. For Jesus Himself, upon whom she leans and who makes her white, says to His disciples: "Without me ye can do nothing" (Jn 15:5).]

Perhaps this amazement did not seize the world only, but overwhelmed the heavenly beings themselves as they see what the human being attains through his union with the Lord Christ in the font of Baptism, that is, they see him in his new birth bearing the possibility of ascending toward the heavens in white garments. As St. Cyril of Jerusalem described man in Baptism, saying: [The angels dance around you, saying, "Who is this that cometh up white in her garments, leaning upon her near one?" For the soul that was formerly a slave has been adopted by her Master and made near to Him.] The heavenly beings also repeat the following saying:
"I raised thee up (lifted thee) under the apple tree: there thy mother brought thee forth: there she brought thee forth that bare thee" [5].
This is the secret of her coming up from the wilderness all white, leaning upon her beloved: that her mother brought her forth and she that bare her gave her birth under the apple tree.

We have seen before that the "apple tree" signifies the divine Incarnation, for the Lord appeared "as the apple tree among the trees of the wood" (Song 2:3). Through the divine Incarnation the Mother Church was able to bear children to God in Baptism, able to rise toward the heavens through the incarnate God... This is the new birth, and this is its power in the life of the believers.

Here there is a link between the divine Incarnation and our spiritual birth, for the Lord was born bodily so that we may be born spiritually. And this is the secret of celebrating the feasts of the Nativity and of Baptism (Theophany) on one day in the early Church..., for the two feasts are bound together in the mind of the Church.

entries.section: Not being preoccupied with service at the expense of the Bridegroom:

paragraphs.text: The working bride affirms her clinging to her Bridegroom in the midst of her preoccupation with serving her neighbor, saying:
"Set me as a seal (stamp) upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave (the tomb).
The coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame of the Lord.
Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.
If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned" [6-7].

If the soul has enjoyed the new birth under the apple tree through Baptism, and in the sacrament of the Myron was sealed with the seal of the Holy Spirit, so that she became the possession of the Bridegroom, bearing His seal and His marks, then she cherishes this seal which has become hers in every aspect of her life. This life kindles the flame of her love toward Him, so she asks Him not merely to receive her between His arms or to take her in His eternal embrace, but she longs to cling to Him like a seal upon His heart and His arm, that not even death may separate her from Him!

She asks to be a seal upon the heart of the Bridegroom. She does not ask merely to have a place in His heart, but to occupy the whole heart, as though God were preoccupied with her alone. She wants not that her name be engraved upon His heart, but that she with all her life be sealed upon it, so that no one can approach or erase her name from before the face of God.
In the book of the prophet Isaiah the Lord says: "Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands" (Isa 49:16), but here the bride asks to be a seal upon His arm...

Thus the bride settles in the heart of God, "the center of affection and love", and in His arm, "the center of work", resting forever upon the throne of His love and upon the seat of His power! This is the boldness of the Church before her Bridegroom!

The secret of this strong boldness is the love which the Lord has poured into our hearts toward Him. Therefore she says: "Love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave..." as though she were saying to Him: Death is trivial, it cannot separate me from my love for You, and the many waters and all the floods cannot quench it or drown it. As the Apostle Paul says: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?... For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Rom 8:38-39).

St. Augustine says: [The storms of the world or the waves of trials cannot quench the flame of love. Of this it was said: "Love is strong as death". For just as when death comes there is none who can resist it, since those who are born to die cannot repel the violence of death by any art or any kind of medicine, so the world cannot stand against the power of love.
He took the comparison from the example of death, its opposite: as death is violent in destroying, so love is strong in rescuing (saving).
Through love many have died to the world that they might live to God.]

In the midst of the world the bride offered to her Bridegroom what the world cannot resist; she offered her heart to Him who finds His delight in the heart. She did not stop at the limits of offering service, striving and vigils, but first offered her heart, that is, all her "love", of which she says: "If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned". It is as though she were repeating what the Apostle Paul said: "Though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing" (1 Cor 13:3).

She is not like the wife who thinks she serves her husband well, so she spends all her effort in serving the house and gives him her body... but her heart is not with him! She offers the heart first, and through it she cannot refrain from serving him!

entries.section: Her love for her Bridegroom kindles her love for her brethren:

paragraphs.text: When she offered all her love to the Lord, her heart was enlarged for her brethren, so she rose to seek on their behalf, saying:
"We have a little sister, and she hath no breasts:
what shall we do for our sister in the day when she shall be spoken for?!
If she be a wall, we will build upon her a palace of silver: and if she be a door, we will enclose her with boards of cedar.
I am a wall, and my breasts like towers: then was I in his eyes as one that found peace" [8-10].

These simple expressions carry a constitution for the life of service, whose articles are summarized in the following points: 1. Realizing the position of unbelievers in relation to the Church, that they represent the "little sister", who is not only her sister, but is a sister to the Bridegroom as well as to the bride. In this view the Church does not deal with unbelievers, even those who trouble her or oppose the truth... even if they are atheists, on the level of a teacher with a pupil, but rather of the elder sister who is gentle with the younger. The younger sister may wrong the elder, so let the other bear with her because she is "the elder", and let her give her an excuse because the younger "hath no breasts"... that is, she has not discovered the truth through the two Testaments. 2. The secret of the weakness of the younger is that she has no breasts, so the work of the elder is to offer the word of God, that is, the Old and New Testaments, so that the little sister may taste them and love them and acquire them as her two breasts. This is the evangelistic work of the Church... offering the living word of God to every person. 3. What does the Church do for the little sister, when the Bridegroom has sought her as one betrothed, and she is without breasts?! Let her deal with her with all sympathy and love, not reproaching her or wounding her feelings, but being gentle with her and offering her every possibility. For if the younger be a wall, she builds upon her a palace of silver, and if she be a door, she encloses her with boards of cedar... She supports her with positive work.

The elder sister offers herself and her life to the younger, saying to her: If you are in need of a wall to surround you and two towers to lift you up... I am at your service: "I am a wall, and my breasts like towers". Receive the Lord Christ who is within me as a wall for you, and my Holy Bible as two breasts to satisfy you. 4. The matter does not stop at treating what is lacking in the life of the little sister who has no breasts, but the elder builds upon her a palace of silver and encloses her with boards of cedar... as though she supports her sister until she becomes a working servant in the vineyard of the Lord. The work of the Church is to bring unbelievers into the faith and urge them to practical witness to the word of God before others... Thus they become like the palace of silver (silver signifies the word of God refined like silver, and the palace signifies open witness).
Thus the Church becomes in the eyes of all as one that found true peace in the life of mankind.

entries.section: Closing dialogue:

paragraphs.text: "Solomon had a vineyard at Baalhamon; he let out the vineyard unto keepers (guards); every one for the fruit thereof was to bring a thousand pieces of silver. My vineyard, which is mine, is before me: thou, O Solomon, must have a thousand, and those that keep the fruit thereof two hundred.
Thou that dwellest in the gardens, the companions hearken to thy voice: cause me to hear it.

Make haste, my beloved, and be thou like to a roe or to a young hart (a young one) upon the mountains of spices" [11-14]. 1. As the Church enters with the world to her Bridegroom the Lord Christ... she calls all to enjoy Him, and here the Church makes clear an important principle in service: the vineyard is the vineyard of Christ, and He is the one who works in it through the vinedressers. Therefore she says: "Solomon had a vineyard at Baalhamon". The vineyard is not her vineyard, but the vineyard of the "true Solomon"...

In this St. Augustine says: [God cultivates us, His vineyard... Our planting is the work that is in our hearts, and He does not work with human hands. He cultivates us as the husbandman does his field. The Lord says in the Gospel: "I am the vine, ye are the branches... my Father is the husbandman" (Jn 15:1, 5). And what does the husbandman do? He cultivates his field. So God the Father is a husbandman who has a field which He cultivates, and from which He expects fruit. And the Lord Jesus Christ Himself says that a man "planted a vineyard... and let it out to husbandmen"; these are bound to render the fruits in their seasons.]

St. John Chrysostom also says, commenting on the saying of the Apostle: ["For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building" (1 Cor 3:9)... The field is not ascribed to him who sows in it but to its owner.] 2. The word "Baal" means "lord" or "king", and "Hamon" means "multitude". It is as though the vineyard of the Lord Christ, the King of Peace, is the multitudes of mankind... He becomes King of these multitudes to bring them into His heavens. 3. The Lord has let out this vineyard to vinedressers... "he let out the vineyard unto keepers", but He does not cease to care for the vineyard Himself and to look after it in great love, for He says, "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me". He guards it Himself night and day (Isa 27:1-3), and does not withhold anything from it, even saying in reproach: "Judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it?!" (Isa 5:3-4). 4. What is the fruit that the King of Peace asks for? "Every one for the fruit thereof was to bring a thousand pieces of silver". This is what He asks of the vinedressers, that all bring thousands, because the thousand signifies heaven and the heavenly life. For God will accept from the servants only spiritual, heavenly fruit. This is the work of the Church and the mission of the servants of the word... to bring those they serve into the heavenly life. 5. If the fruit is rendered for the account of the Lord Christ, what is the share of the servants? "Thou, O Solomon, must have a thousand, and those that keep the fruit thereof two hundred". Perhaps by the two hundred he meant one hundred for the men of the Old Testament and one hundred for the men of the New Testament, for the fruit is abundant and all the servants in both Testaments enjoy it. Therefore the Apostle Paul says to his people: "my joy and crown" (Phil 4:1). 6. As the Church works in the vineyard of the Lord, and the workers realize that they work for the account of the Lord Christ, who has "the thousand", and also for their own account, for they have "the two hundred", they become like those who are in the midst of gardens. The narrow gate and the afflicted way are transformed into an easy yoke and a light burden. They live while on earth as in joyful paradises, so the Lord speaks to His bride, saying: "Thou that dwellest in the gardens, the companions hearken to thy voice: cause me to hear it". The voice of your love is no longer muffled, but those on earth hear it, as the heavenly beings rejoice in it... And now come to Me that I may hear your joyful, practical voice, come, "inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world" (Mt 25:34).
These are the words of a Bridegroom who gladdens the heart of His bride, and assures her that what she does will receive its fruits on an eternal level.

She answers Him with joy, saying: "Make haste (hurry), my beloved, and be thou like to a roe or to a young hart (a young one) upon the mountains of spices". We have already seen why the Church likens her Bridegroom to the roe and to the young harts... Here she responds to His call, saying: Hasten to me and come, for I long for You... If You call me to meet You that You may hear my voice, then I also need to meet You.

And perhaps His coming in haste upon the mountain of spices reminds us of the spices with which the Lord was shrouded, for He meets her through her burial with Him... as she dies with Him every day, that she may live with Him forever.
This is the conclusion of the Song... as though she were repeating what the bride said in the book of the Apocalypse (Revelation): "Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus"!
